### Grabs, shoves and close-quarters mechanics

<a id="close-quarters-combat-rework"></a>

Reworks hands-on combat with escalating grabs, shove impacts, tackles, knockdowns, backstabs, point-blank executions and a contest system that resolves who wins.

**rmc14**

*loop-change · entangled · medium confidence · 11 forks carry it*

Shoving stops being a one-shot coin flip and becomes a wrestling match: you barge into someone repeatedly, each attempt announcing itself to everyone nearby ("you try to tackle X", "X tackles you down"), and after a few failed shoves the next one is guaranteed to slam them flat and paralyse them for a couple of seconds. Anyone knocked down, stunned, unconscious or freshly tackled can be rescued by a buddy grabbing them with an empty hand and shaking them, which shaves seconds off the timer and pops them back upright, though someone whose stamina is gone just flops straight back down. Shoving an armed person while untrained in close-quarters combat can make their gun go off by accident, and being dazed drops a dark vignette over your screen that squeezes how far you can see, while wielding a gun paints a crosshair on your cursor and targeting lasers visibly mark whoever they are painted on.

- **Take** — It turns shoving from a random stun into a legible back-and-forth with escalating odds and a teammate-driven counterplay (shaking someone awake), so hands-on fights become a group activity rather than a coin flip.
- **Skip** — The tackle path is gated on RMC's own skills, stamina, standing/rest and xeno-infection systems and fires off a fork-replaced disarm event, so grafting it means either dragging those systems along or rewriting the contest rules against upstream's disarm and stamina model.
- **Touches** — all-players, security, antagonist, medical
- **Needs** — [squads-ranks-and-skills](#squads-ranks-and-skills), [xenomorph-hive](#xenomorph-hive), [mob-damage-and-movement](#mob-damage-and-movement)
- **Verified** — partly supported. Core mechanics check out against the source: TackleSystem.cs confirms the Min=2/Max=6/Chance=0.35 escalating-attempt-to-guaranteed-paralysis loop and PVS popups; StunShakeableSystem.cs confirms the shake-awake rescue (clears Stun/KnockedDown/Unconscious/TackledRecentlyBy, blocked by stamina crit); RMCDisarmComponent+TackleSystem confirm the untrained-CQC accidental-discharge-on-shove mechanic gated on skill 'RMCSkillCqc'. But the claim overclaims by presenting the escalating 'wrestling match' as generic all-player shoving: entity YAML shows TackleComponent lives only on Xeno/base_xeno.yml (xenomorph-only attacker), while Tackleable sits on Species/base.yml and simplemob.yml (marines/NPCs as victims only) -- ordinary marine-vs-marine shoving instead runs the separate RMCDisarm/RMCDisarmable percentage roll, which has no memory of prior attempts and never escalates to a guaranteed knockdown. The claim also folds in the dazed vignette (RMCDazedComponent) and the crosshair/targeting laser (RMCCombatModeSystem/TargetingComponent) as if part of this loop, but a repo-wide grep shows Dazed is applied/removed by unrelated xeno abilities (XenoSacrificeHealActionEvent, XenoFightOrFlightComponent) and neither crosshair nor laser-targeting code is referenced anywhere in Tackle/Disarm/ShakeStun -- these are separate combat-feel systems, not wired into this feature. On graft_shape: the seed's 'drop-in' is clearly wrong and the assessor's 'entangled' downgrade is correct, and understated if anything -- beyond the cited skills/xeno-infection/stamina dependencies, I found the fork has directly patched an UPSTREAM file, Content.Shared/Weapons/Melee/SharedMeleeWeaponSystem.cs (outside any _RMC14 directory), inside DoDisarm() to raise 'new CMDisarmEvent(user)' alongside the vanilla DisarmedEvent -- TackleSystem's entire trigger path depends on that in-place upstream edit, which the path-data evidence list (all _RMC14-namespaced files) never surfaced. That is exactly the class of upstream in-place edit the seed's path data cannot see, and it independently confirms this unit is not remotely drop-in.
  - unsupported: "Shoving stops being a one-shot coin flip and becomes a wrestling match: you barge into someone repeatedly, each attempt announcing itself to everyone nearby... and after a few failed shoves the next one is guaranteed to slam them flat and paralyse them" -- this escalating/guaranteed-knockdown behavior belongs to the Tackle/Tackleable pair, which per Resources/Prototypes/_RMC14/Entities/Mobs is exclusively a xenomorph-attacks-marine mechanic (Tackle only on Xeno/base_xeno.yml); ordinary marine-on-marine shoving runs the separate RMCDisarm/RMCDisarmable percentage roll with no attempt memory and no guaranteed-knockdown escalation, so describing generic 'shoving' this way overstates what player-vs-player shoving actually does.
  - unsupported: "being dazed drops a dark vignette over your screen that squeezes how far you can see" -- RMCDazedComponent/RMCDazedSystem do implement this vision effect, but nothing in TackleSystem, the RMCDisarm handlers, or StunShakeableSystem applies or removes the Dazed status; the only code paths touching it (XenoSacrificeHealActionEvent, XenoFightOrFlightComponent) are unrelated xeno abilities, so bundling it into this 'close-quarters combat' narrative is unsupported by the cited files.
  - unsupported: "wielding a gun paints a crosshair on your cursor and targeting lasers visibly mark whoever they are painted on" -- RMCCombatModeSystem.GetCrosshair and TargetingComponent exist and do this, but neither is referenced anywhere in the Tackle/Disarm/ShakeStun code; they are separate wielding/targeting-device features folded into the claim without any wiring evidence connecting them to the shove/tackle mechanic.

**starlight**

*loop-change · entangled · medium confidence · 11 forks carry it*

Standing over someone who is cuffed or already down, a right-click option appears to finish them off with a sharp weapon or a loaded gun: a short wind-up prints a message everyone nearby can read, and if nobody interrupts it, the victim dies. Aimed at yourself, the same option becomes a suicide. Heavy guns now shove the person firing them, throwing you backwards a tile or two and draining stamina with each shot unless you are wearing magboots, and examining the weapon tells you in advance how far it will push you and how much stamina that costs. Melee weapons can carry payloads that inject chemicals into whoever they connect with or clamp cuffs onto a target after a brief struggle, and shots that fail to punch through armour throw off sparks and a ricochet clang instead of wounding you. Despite the feature name, this bundle is not a grab or shove rework, there is no escalating grab ladder here.

- **Take** — Executions and shooter recoil both make fights feel decisive rather than attritional, and the on-hit payload components are a cheap generic hook any fork can hang new weapons off (chem syringe batons, capture guns) without writing new systems.
- **Skip** — It is a grab-bag rather than the coherent close-quarters rework the name promises, and several pieces (armour sparks, pierce levels, friction status, stun baton visuals) are written against Starlight's own ballistics and stun rework, so grafting them means either dragging that in too or rewriting them against upstream hitscan and SharedStunSystem.
- **Touches** — security, antagonist, all-players, medical
- **Needs** — [firearms-content-expansion](#firearms-content-expansion)
- **Verified** — partly supported; assessed as needs upstream edits, corrected by the verifier. Beyond what the claim states, I found the fork does not merely need upstream edits to integrate — its own tree already patches at least three vanilla-path files in place: Content.Shared/Execution/ExecutionComponent.cs (marked \"//STARLIGHT MODIFIED FILE ... TODO: Use upstream and modify it accordingly instead\", converting instance fields to statics and splitting Melee/Gun variants that vanilla's current ExecutionComponent.cs does not have), Content.Shared/Weapons/Ranged/Systems/SharedGunSystem.cs (adds the OnNonEmptyGunShotEvent the knockback system depends on — not even in the cited evidence list), and Content.Shared/Stunnable/SharedStunSystem.cs (extensive \"// Starlight edit start/end\" blocks adding a voluntary-knockdown parameter, referenced via FrictionStatusComponent's Access(typeof(SharedStunSystem)) restriction). Combined with ArmorSparkEffectComponent's own doc comment tying it to Starlight's own SP/HP ammo pierce levels, this is a bundle threaded through the fork's own ballistics and stun rework plus three separately-modified vanilla files, not a clean self-contained needs-upstream-edits unit.
  - unsupported: "unless you are wearing magboots" — the cited SharedKnockbackSystem.cs only checks for a generic NoSlipComponent (worn item or self) via CheckForNoSlips(); no cited file or YAML ties that component specifically to magboots, and none of the cited files name which item grants it.
  - unsupported: "Heavy guns now shove the person firing them" — the mechanic is driven by KnockbackByUserTagComponent matching arbitrary TagPrototype keys in a dictionary; no cited evidence shows this is restricted to a 'heavy guns' category as opposed to any tagged weapon.

### Ship-to-ship combat

<a id="ship-to-ship-combat"></a>

Vessel-scale warfare: crew-served ship guns wired to fire-control and gunnery consoles, guided missiles, radar contacts, armour plating, cloaking and thermal detection.

**monolith**

*structural · needs upstream edits · medium confidence · 3 forks carry it*

Ships fight other ships. A gunner sits at a gunnery control console wired to a gunnery server, selects which of the ship's turrets are live, and fires by aiming the cursor on the console map, so a turret only shoots when the target is inside its arc and someone has to fly the ship to bring guns to bear while someone else pulls the trigger. Three weapon families exist: ballistic autocannons and railguns that burn cartridges, energy guns with effectively unlimited shots, and guided missiles that lock onto any grid carrying a shuttle console and can reach well past what the turrets themselves can see. Ballistic and missile mounts need ammunition hauled to them, a pneumatic ammo loader can be multitool-linked to up to eight guns to feed them, and loose ammo is volatile if it gets hit. Meanwhile your ship is broadcasting: firing guns, running thrusters, powering generators and charging an FTL drive all raise a thermal signature that decides how far off enemies see you on radar, while a cloaking device hides you until its heat gauge climbs from Low to Critical and trips an overheat lockout with a visible countdown. Enemy vessels can also be crewed by NPC ship AI that steers and shoots on its own. Bundled in the same unit is a personal armour-plate system: carriers take insertable plates with their own durability that shatter when spent, absorb or amplify specific damage types, convert part of what they soak into stamina damage, and slow your walk or sprint by weight.

- **Take** — It is a complete, documented, player-facing vessel-combat package: gunnery consoles and servers, three weapon families, guided missiles, ammo loaders, radar/thermal detection, cloaking with heat management and NPC ship AI, all shipped with an in-game guidebook already written for players.
- **Skip** — It only pays off in a fork where players already crew their own ships in a shared sector; on a single-station round there is nothing to shoot at, and the 244 files bring a second combat balance surface (turret arcs, missile ranges, thermal signatures, armour plates) that has to be tuned and maintained forever.
- **Touches** — command, security, engineering, cargo, all-players
- **Needs** — [shipyard-player-ships](#shipyard-player-ships)
- **Verified** — supported. Fetched all 9 cited files and they back the gameplay description closely: gunnery.ftl/shipguns.ftl confirm the console+server+FOV gating, ShipCombat.xml confirms the 3 weapon families and missile-vs-turret range gap, ammo_loader.yml literally supports 8 guns via multitool link, cloak-heat.ftl shows the Low/Medium/High/Critical gauge and overheat lockout timer, armor-plate.ftl confirms durability/shatter/absorb-amplify/stamina/speed mechanics, and ThermalSignatureSystem.cs subscribes to gun shots, thrusters, power suppliers, and FTL drives for signature. Critically, I pulled the upstream file Content.Shared/Weapons/Ranged/Components/GunComponent.cs directly (not in the evidence list, not under any _Mono path) and found it edited in place with a '// Mono' tagged field 'public float ShootThermalSignature = 0f;' plus several other Mono-tagged additions (recoil, execution-time fields). That proves the feature's implementation patches an upstream file rather than staying confined to _Mono namespace directories, so the claim's downgrade from the seed's 'drop-in' guess to 'needs-upstream-edits' is correct, specifically in the fork-patches-upstream sense (not merely 'would need edits if grafted elsewhere').

**rmc14**

*loop-change · entangled · high confidence · 3 forks carry it*

Rather than ships shooting at each other, RMC-14's version is off-map artillery: a crew-served mortar you deploy on the ground and a giant orbital cannon sitting on the ship. A spotter lases a target with a rangefinder or laser designator, calls grid coordinates over the radio, and the mortar operator types those X/Y numbers into the mortar's screen and drops in a shell — high explosive to stun and flatten, incendiary to set a burning wall across a retreat route, or a flare shell that plants a camera and gives you a live 19x19 view of where you are shooting. Range is capped between 15 and 65 tiles, shots drift further out the longer the throw, and each time you re-set coordinates the gun picks a fresh hidden aim error you have to walk in using the offset controls, so a good crew fires a camera shell first and corrects from the feed. The orbital cannon is the same idea at a much bigger scale: ship-side crew use a power loader exosuit to haul solid fuel and a warhead onto the loading tray, chamber it at a console, and a lased target planetside then eats an enormous explosion, a diamond of blue fire, a cluster barrage, or the experimental KRAKEN warhead that broadcasts range warnings to everyone nearby before it lands. Each round randomises how much fuel a given warhead needs, so the loading crew has to work it out rather than memorise it.

- **Take** — It creates a genuine two-person job loop, a spotter calling coordinates and a gunner walking rounds onto them over radio, which is one of the few things in SS14 that makes long-range violence a communication exercise instead of a click.
- **Skip** — It is built for RMC-14's marines-versus-xenos planet format and leans on that fork's skill gates, squad radio keys, laser designators, power loader exosuits, planet/area system and custom explosion code, so the mortar and especially the orbital cannon arrive dragging most of a military campaign game with them; a station round with 65-tile firing lanes and a ship-mounted bombardment target is not obviously a thing that exists.
- **Touches** — security, command, engineering, cargo, antagonist, all-players
- **Needs** — [squads-ranks-and-skills](#squads-ranks-and-skills), [explosion-rework](#explosion-rework), [mech-overhaul](#mech-overhaul)
- **Verified** — supported. Read the mortar guidebook (confirms 15-65 tile range, HE/incendiary/flare shells with 19x19 camera view, coordinate+offset system with hidden per-set aim error, JTAC/laser-designator spotting) and the orbital cannon C# system + prototypes (confirms power-loader tray loading, console Load/Unload/Chamber UI, per-round randomized fuel-per-warhead via PickAndTake, Explosive/Cluster/Incendiary/Aegis(KRAKEN) warheads with the exact 'diamond of ultra-hot blue fire' and staged range-warning broadcasts before Aegis detonation). Every specific claim in the gameplay text is directly traceable to source. The orbital cannon system also imports Areas, ARES, Marines.Squads, PowerLoader, Mortar, Rules, and a custom RMCExplosionSystem, which confirms genuine entanglement with the fork's other systems (squad/skill gates, mech/power-loader, planet-area, custom explosions) rather than a self-contained drop-in, correctly overriding the path-data 'drop-in' seed guess.

**serbia-strong**

*loop-change · needs upstream edits · medium confidence · 3 forks carry it*

This fork adds a gunnery console for a ship's mounted guns. A crewmate links the ship's guns to the console, opens it, and gets a radar-style view of the surrounding space; clicking a spot on that map swings every linked gun around to face it, and a dedicated fire key lets the gunner volley them all at once without running between weapons. A reset button snaps the guns back to the rotation they started at, and guns whose line of fire is blocked by the ship's own hull simply do not fire, so a gunner cannot shoot through their own walls.

- **Take** — Turns scattered ship guns into a single aimable battery a lone gunner can actually operate mid-fight, which is the difference between shuttle weapons being decoration and being a real combat role.
- **Skip** — It is only the aiming-and-firing console, not the rest of a ship combat layer, so it is worth little unless your maps already carry mounted guns and hostile ships worth pointing them at; it also claims its own keybind context, which means a new key function and a keybind entry to maintain.
- **Touches** — command, cargo, security, antagonist
- **Verified** — supported. Every specific mechanic in the gameplay text checks out in the actual source: DeviceListUpdateEvent builds the linked-gun list, RequestRotateGunToPoint/RotateToPoint swing every linked gun to a clicked point, FireShuttle is a real added key-function wired into ShuttleNavControl's KeyBindDown/Up and FrameUpdate to volley-fire while held, RequestResetRotateShuttleGuns restores each gun's ShuttleGunRecords starting angle, and CanShoot raycasts against the shuttle's own grid so hull-blocked guns refuse to fire. But the seed's drop-in guess is wrong in exactly the way it warned about: grepping the full tarball turns up "SS220 add additional control for shuttle" edits baked directly into upstream Content.Server/Shuttles/Components/ShuttleConsoleComponent.cs, Content.Server/Shuttles/Systems/ShuttleConsoleSystem.cs, Content.Client/Shuttles/UI/ShuttleNavControl.xaml.cs and NavScreen.xaml(.cs) - the "gunnery console" is not a standalone new UI, it's the vanilla piloting radar screen (NavScreen/ShuttleNavControl) conditionally augmented with a gun-control widget and a CanControlShuttle=false flag on a new console prototype. The claim's own "needs-upstream-edits" downgrade from the drop-in seed is therefore correct, and it is the strong fork-patches-upstream flavor, not merely a hypothetical integration cost.

### Gun attachments and upgrade kits

<a id="gun-attachments-and-upgrades"></a>

Modular parts fitted to firearms through a dedicated slot UI: rails, barrels, underbarrels, silencers and installable kits that change damage, range or handling.

**ephemeral-space, far-horizons, rmc14**

*loop-change · needs upstream edits · medium confidence · 2 forks carry it*

You can fit parts onto a gun instead of being stuck with the gun you were issued: click a scope, silencer, foregrip or extended barrel onto the weapon and it drops into a named slot (rail, barrel, underbarrel), with a small panel on the gun showing which slots are filled and letting you pop a part back out. Examining a gun tells you what is currently bolted to it, and the gun's behaviour changes to match — quieter or different firing sound, altered accuracy, recoil, damage, melee bash, how long it takes to wield, and how fast you move while carrying it. RMC-14's version goes furthest: attachments show up as sprite layers on the weapon, some are toggled on and off in place (fold a bipod, deploy a stock), some lock you to a facing or stop you firing while deployed, and there are IFF and prying attachments; Far Horizons only adds a handful of craftable revolver barrel kits rather than a framework.

- **Take** — It turns every firearm into something a player customises and invests in, giving security, cargo and antags a whole new axis of loot and preparation without adding a single new gun.
- **Skip** — The framework is worthless until you also edit upstream weapon prototypes to declare slots and author a whole catalogue of attachments, and every stat modifier is a new balance surface to tune and re-tune against upstream gun changes.
- **Touches** — security, antagonist, cargo, all-players
- **Verified** — supported. Read the actual C#/YAML for all three forks: ES's ESAttachableGunComponent/ESGunSoundAttachmentComponent/ESSharedGunAttachmentsSystem and RMC-14's AttachableModifiersSystem partials (Ranged/Melee/Speed/WieldDelay) plus rmc_attachable_base/holder.yml and under_attachments.yml (bipod) confirm essentially every specific claim: named slots (rail/barrel/stock/underbarrel tags), sound swap on silencer, accuracy/recoil/damage/scatter/fire-rate modifiers, melee bonus damage, wield-delay change, walk/sprint speed change, sprite layering (AttachableVisuals, iconActive), in-place toggle (bipod fold/deploy), IFF (AttachableIFFComponent) and prying (AttachablePryingComponent) attachments, and Far Horizons' attachments.yml really is just four revolver-barrel construction recipes, not a framework. On graft shape: sparse-cloning both repos shows the attachment components are only ever applied to each fork's own namespaced gun prototypes (_ES/Entities/Objects/Weapons/Guns/*, _RMC14/Entities/Objects/Weapons/Guns/Attachments/*) — RMC-14 still carries an untouched upstream Resources/Prototypes/Entities/Objects/Weapons folder with zero Attachable references, and ES has deleted the upstream Weapons folder entirely and reimplemented every gun under _ES. So the fork copies are self-contained (not fork-patches-upstream), but grafting this onto a codebase that still has its normal upstream gun prototypes (like honksquad) would require adding the attachment component to those existing prototypes or replacing them — confirming the claim's needs-upstream-edits / integration-would-require-upstream-edits reading.
  - unsupported: "some lock you to a facing" — RMC's AttachableToggleableComponent only has BreakOnRotate/BreakOnFullRotate flags, which deactivate the attachment's bonus if you turn away; nothing in the code actually restricts/locks the player's facing input itself, so "lock you to a facing" overstates a softer "the buff cancels if you rotate" mechanic.

### Martial arts

<a id="martial-arts"></a>

Learnable unarmed fighting styles with combo inputs that chain into throws, table slams, disarms and finishers, taught by manuals or granted by antag roles. Covers only the martial-art styles themselves; a vendored `MartialArts/` directory sitting next to unrelated siblings does not pull those siblings in with it.

**goobstation, serbia-strong**

*loop-change · needs upstream edits · high confidence · 4 forks carry it*

A character who has learned a fighting style stops throwing plain punches and starts chaining moves: attack, grab and shove inputs performed in a specific order on the same target within a few seconds fire a named finisher instead of a normal hit, with a message like "You hit Urist with Slam". Goob ships eight styles (CQC, Corporate Judo, Krav Maga, Sleeping Carp, Capoeira, Ninjutsu, Dragon Kung Fu, Hell Ripte) with distinct move lists, so a chef with CQC can slam someone to the floor for twelve seconds or drain their stamina to zero in two inputs, a Sleeping Carp master shouts "COWABUNGA!" while slashing, and a capoeira fighter has to be sprinting for kicks to land. Styles are taught by a manual or scroll that burns up once read, only one style per person sticks, and some are locked behind conditions (learning CQC as chef only works in the kitchen until you are freed of that restriction; changelings simply refuse). SS220's version is a smaller take on the same idea: two styles (CQC and Corporate Judo) built from configurable step sequences, plus passive perks like faster grabs, higher disarm chance, a leg sweep, an eye poke that blinds an unprotected target, and a judo throw that flattens a standing victim.

- **Take** — It turns unarmed fighting from spam-click-until-crit into a small input game with real depth, and gives departments and antags a memorable identity without adding a single new weapon.
- **Skip** — Both implementations hang off a fork-specific grab/shove pipeline (SS220 sequences set grab stages and chokeholds; Goob's combo events must be raised from patched melee, disarm and pull code), so the balance and the plumbing both have to be re-tuned against your own combat rules rather than dropped in.
- **Touches** — security, service, antagonist, all-players
- **Needs** — [close-quarters-combat-rework](#close-quarters-combat-rework)
- **Verified** — partly supported. Fetched the Goob-Station git tree and grepped for ComboAttackPerformedEvent: it's raised from Content.Shared/Weapons/Melee/SharedMeleeWeaponSystem.cs (lines 696-697, 883-884, 1064-1065, 1081-1082) for Harm/HarmLight/Disarm attacks — that file lives in the core Content.Shared namespace, not under any _Goobstation/Content.Goobstation.* directory, and it has been directly patched in place to raise martial-arts combo events. That is a real fork-patches-upstream edit the path data (which apparently only scanned _Goobstation/SS220 namespaced paths) missed, so the "drop-in" seed is wrong and the claim's downgrade to needs-upstream-edits is correct. Grab-type combo events are raised from Content.Goobstation.Shared/GrabIntent/GrabIntentSystem.GrabStages.cs, which is self-contained fork code but itself depends on the fork's separate grab-stage/chokehold system (matching the claim's depends_on: close-quarters-combat-rework) — so wiring this into a different codebase would also require patching that codebase's own melee system the same way Goob patched its upstream file, making both upstream_reading senses true simultaneously.
  - unsupported: "a judo throw that flattens a standing victim" and "an eye poke that blinds an unprotected target" are listed alongside "faster grabs, higher disarm chance, a leg sweep" as SS220's 'passive perks' — but in ss_corporate_judo.yml/ss_cqc.yml the throw, armbar, discombobulate and eye-poke are all entries under `sequences:` (steps: [Push, Harm] / [Grab, Push] etc.), i.e. active input-order combos exactly like Goob's, not passive perks. Only grabDelayCoefficient, DisarmChanceMartialArtEffect, LegSweepMartialArtEffect and BonusDamageMartialArtEffect sit under the martialArt's `effects:` block and are actually passive.
  - unsupported: "a chef with CQC can ... drain their stamina to zero in two inputs" — CQCPressure (Disarm+Grab, 2 attacks) only deals staminaDamage: 65 and CQCConsecutive (which actually needs 3 attacks: Disarm, Disarm, Harm) deals 70; neither combo's own extraDamage/staminaDamage field zeroes a full stamina bar by itself in the files, only in combination with unlisted base disarm/grab stamina costs.
  - unsupported: "a capoeira fighter has to be sprinting for kicks to land" generalizes to all capoeira kicks, but in gb_capoeira.yml only SweepKick and SpinKick carry `minVelocity: 2`; PushKick, CircleKick and KickUp have no velocity gate.

### Modular hardsuits (modsuits)

<a id="modular-hardsuits"></a>

Deployable suits that unfold piece by piece over the wearer and accept craftable modules, replacing one-piece hardsuits.

**gaby-station-now-dumont-station, sunrise**

*loop-change · entangled · medium confidence · 4 forks carry it*

Instead of one sealed hardsuit, you get a suit that comes apart into pieces: a chestplate, helmet, gloves and boots you seal up with a mechanical clunk when you need to go outside, in mining, engineering, paramedic and security flavours printed at a lathe for a chunk of steel, gold and silver. Each piece has a socket, and you fit small printed modules into it to change what the suit does for you: jump boots, magboots or clown shoes in the feet, a mining drill or a surgical omnitool in the gloves, med/sec/diagnostic HUDs and welding protection in the helmet, and anti-gravity, a GPS or an auto-injector that dumps healing chems into you the moment you crit in the chest. Sunrise's take instead has you wear the suit as a backpack that unfolds over you on command, keyed to you at round start so nobody else can wear it, with an emergency compartment holding an ampoule of chemicals you can inject through the suit without ever unsealing.

- **Take** — It turns hardsuits from a single "do you have one or not" item into an ongoing kit-building decision, and gives science and the wearer something to do with the suit all round.
- **Skip** — Neither implementation stands alone: Dumont's modules ride on the Goob-style gun-upgrade modkit system and its armour and surgical-tool modules assume the limb-wound/surgery rework, while Sunrise's version needs its own modsuit C# system plus sponsor-gated loadouts, so you would be porting the scaffolding before you ever see a module.
- **Touches** — engineering, medical, security, cargo, science, all-players
- **Needs** — [gun-attachments-and-upgrades](#gun-attachments-and-upgrades), [surgery-and-limb-wounds](#surgery-and-limb-wounds), [loadout-system](#loadout-system), [sponsor-and-donator-perks](#sponsor-and-donator-perks)
- **Verified** — partly supported. I re-fetched every cited file plus several uncited ones needed to settle the flavour/lathe question. Dumont side: modules.yml comment explicitly says the module system reuses the PKA gun-upgrade modkit system (GunUpgrade/GunUpgradeComponents), confirming the gun-attachments dependency; chestplate Armor blocks carry Dismemberment/OrganDamage/BoneDamage traumaDeductions, confirming the surgery/limb-wound dependency; every specific module named in the claim (jump, magboot, clownshoes, drill, diamond drill, surgical, medhud, diagnostichud, sechud, welding, antigrav, GPS, crit-injector) exists with matching slot tags and behavior. But the base modsuit entity and the Engineer/Paramedic/Security chestplates actually live in _Goobstation/Entities/Clothing/OuterClothing/modsuit.yml (a separate vendored fork namespace edited by Gabystation via '# GabyStation begin/end' blocks), and the lathe recipes cited only cover Engineer/Paramedic/Security producing plating-upgrade tags for that older whole-suit system — the Mining flavour that Gabystation's own new piece-based files fully implement has no lathe recipe anywhere in the repo. Sunrise side: backpack form, back slot, roundStartBiocode DNA-locking (verified in ModsuitSystem.cs OnEquip), the emergency-compartment Ampula/inject actions, and sponsorOnly loadouts all check out exactly as described. Net: the seed's drop-in guess is wrong and the assessor's downgrade to entangled is correct — if anything the true picture is more entangled than the claim states, since the feature isn't self-contained even within its own fork's namespace.
  - unsupported: "printed at a lathe for a chunk of steel, gold and silver" in mining, engineering, paramedic and security flavours" — no lathe recipe for the Mining chestplate/helmet exists anywhere in _Gabystation/Recipes/Lathes/ (only ModsuitPlatingEngineerRecipe/ParamedicRecipe/SecurityRecipe exist, all Steel/Gold/Silver), and those three recipes don't even produce the piece-based chestplate entities the claim describes: their output is a plating item consumed by a _Goobstation construction-graph (ModsuitPlating* used as a construction tag) that upgrades a different, older whole-suit entity (e.g. ClothingModsuitEngineer), not the new modular chestplate/helmet/glove/boot pieces.
  - unsupported: The claim implies all four flavours (mining/engineering/paramedic/security) work through the same one piece-based socket system; in fact _Gabystation's own new chestplate+helmet+glove+boot files (Entities/Clothing/{OuterClothing,Head,Hands,Shoes}/modsuit.yml) implement ONLY the Mining flavour end-to-end, while Engineering/Paramedic/Security exist as _Goobstation-vendored whole-suit entities extended with the module socket via a shared parent, meaning the feature's actual footprint spans two vendored fork namespaces (_Gabystation and _Goobstation), not one.

## Engineering

### Research tree and lathe rework

<a id="research-tree-rework"></a>

Replaces the technology console with a different progression model, whether a searchable node graph, new disciplines, per-department fabricators or transferable research disks.

**rmc14**

*structural · entangled · medium confidence · 6 forks carry it*

Instead of researching tech in a lab, the crew earns progress by going out and recovering things: intel documents, uploaded data, retrieved items, analyzed chemical samples, rescued survivors, recovered bodies, and restoring the colony's power and comms. All of that feeds a shared points pool that command spends at a Tech Control console, picking from tiered unlock nodes with icons, prices that climb each time a repeatable node is bought, and some nodes time-locked until later in the round. Buying a node has an immediate round-wide effect rather than adding a lathe recipe: more supply budget, more dropship fabricator budget, an emergency supply drop, a vehicle unlocked, or a fresh squad of reinforcement marines spawning as ghost roles from cryo, each purchase announced station-wide and logged under the buyer's name. Separately, a handful of research data disks can be found and slotted into medical machines to teach an autodoc new procedures (internal bleeding, broken bones, organ damage, parasite extraction) or upgrade a sleeper's chemical range and dialysis.

- **Take** — It converts "research" from a lab minigame into a round-wide objective economy, where everyone's fieldwork buys reinforcements, budget and vehicles that visibly change how the rest of the round goes.
- **Skip** — It is not a tech tree you can lift in isolation: the console is wired into RMC-14's intel objectives, requisitions budget, dropship fabricator, ARES logging, marine announcements, player-count scaling and cryo reinforcement spawners, so grafting it means either importing or re-authoring all of those, and the actual node catalogue is not in prototypes, so every option would have to be rebuilt for your own fork's content.
- **Touches** — command, cargo, medical, ghost-roles, all-players
- **Needs** — [cargo-bounties-and-market](#cargo-bounties-and-market), [gamemaster-and-ghost-roles](#gamemaster-and-ghost-roles), [squads-ranks-and-skills](#squads-ranks-and-skills), [autodoc](#autodoc)
- **Verified** — supported. I fetched all 6 cited files plus IntelSystem.cs and the rmc_intel.yml prototype and confirmed the gameplay claim almost point for point: IntelTechTree.cs has exactly the fields claimed (Documents, UploadData, RetrieveItems, AnalyzeChemicals, RescueSurvivors, RecoverCorpses, ColonyCommunications, ColonyPower, Points, TotalEarned, Tier, Options); IntelSystem.cs increments Points/TotalEarned directly; TechOption.cs has Cost/Increase/Repurchasable/CurrentCost/Icon/TimeLock exactly as described; TechSystem.cs enforces the tier gate, time-lock, repurchase-cost-increase, and purchase logging (marine-wide announcement + ARES log with buyer name); the YAML prototype confirms vehicle unlock (VehicleHumveeARC), budget events, and a 115-minute time-locked nuke node; ServerTechSystem.cs confirms the exact ghost-role cryo-spawn squad (SquadLeader/FireteamLeader, CombatTech, HospitalCorpsman, 2x Rifleman) from TechCryoMarinesEvent; research_upgrades.yml confirms the exact autodoc disk list (internal bleeding, broken bones, organ damage, parasite extraction) and the sleeper chemical/dialysis upgrade. On graft_shape: TechSystem.cs (Shared) itself imports and depends on ARESCoreSystem, DropshipFabricatorSystem, SharedMarineAnnounceSystem, SharedRequisitionsSystem, ScalingSystem and ItemIFFComponent, and ServerTechSystem.cs depends on upstream Ghost Roles plus the fork's Cryostorage and squad-tier marine role prototypes — this is real, confirmed entanglement across many of the fork's other subsystems, not a path-data artifact. I also found one factual error in the claim's own skip_because reasoning: it says 'the actual node catalogue is not in prototypes,' but Resources/Prototypes/_RMC14/Entities/Objects/rmc_intel.yml (not in evidence_cited) defines the entire 5-tier node catalogue — names, costs, icons, time locks, and events — as data. That doesn't change the entangled verdict (the C# system wiring is still the real blocker), but it means the claim's stated reason a node catalogue 'would have to be rebuilt' is wrong; the catalogue is fully data-driven and could in principle be reused/adapted, only the systems it fires into cannot.
  - unsupported: an emergency supply drop — the actual TechLogisticsDeliveryEvent nodes I found deliver specific ordnance (RMCOrbitalCannonWarheadExplosive/Incendiary/Cluster OB rounds, or RMCNuke) via _requisitions.CreateSpecialDelivery, not a generic 'supply drop'; framing it as an emergency supply drop is a loose paraphrase the code doesn't literally support

**backmen**

*loop-change · needs upstream edits · medium confidence · 6 forks carry it*

Science works off a rebuilt research console: a pannable node map of technologies you can recenter, filter to already-researched entries, and click to see a card showing the exact recipes it unlocks and the cost in research points. Instead of just needing enough points, a technology can be gated behind "research 3 more Tier 2 Engineering technologies to reach 75%", and once the station commits to a main discipline the higher tiers of the other disciplines grey out with a message saying that branch is locked. The tree itself is a fork-written progression spread across disciplines for engineering, security/arsenal, cargo, mining, medical, robotics and science, so what each department can eventually build, and in what order, is different from the usual station. Unlocking a technology also gets announced with the name and the points spent, and the package ships alongside a talking Oracle statue that demands specific items ("I demand one syringe! Do not question why!") and pays out in research knowledge when fed.

- **Take** — It turns research from a points-shopping list into a routed choice with real consequences, since committing to a main discipline visibly locks out the deep end of the others and forces science to pick a direction for the round.
- **Skip** — It is not a bolt-on: the fork replaces the whole technology tree and the console UI, so every upstream technology and lathe recipe would need re-slotting into their layout and hand-placed node positions, and every future upstream research change becomes a merge conflict you own forever.
- **Touches** — science, engineering, cargo, security, medical, salvage
- **Needs** — [psionics-and-glimmer](#psionics-and-glimmer)
- **Verified** — partly supported. All the cited fork-namespaced files check out (tier-gating ftl string 'Research N more Tier X ... to reach Y%', discipline-lockout ftl string, unlock-announcement ftl string, Oracle demand strings/entity, recenter/Researched-filter buttons, cost label, 8-discipline prototype list, BkmResearchRequirements.cs implementing exactly the tier% and discipline-lockout logic described). Crucially, I traced the C# dependencies BkmResearchRequirements.cs calls into (TechnologyDatabaseComponent.MainDiscipline, TechDisciplinePrototype.LockoutTier, SharedResearchSystem.GetHighestDisciplineTier, TechnologyPrototype.Position) and fetched those upstream-path files directly: Content.Shared/Research/Components/TechnologyDatabaseComponent.cs, Content.Shared/Research/Prototypes/TechDisciplinePrototype.cs, Content.Shared/Research/Systems/SharedResearchSystem.cs, and Content.Shared/Research/Prototypes/TechnologyPrototype.cs all contain in-place edits (fields/methods added directly, with comments like 'Backmen change:' and 'backmen: rnd-auto-layout'). This proves the fork's own tree already patches upstream files in place (fork-patches-upstream), on top of the separately-true fact that wiring in every upstream recipe/technology would require further upstream edits (integration-would-require-upstream-edits) — hence both. This confirms needs-upstream-edits is correct and the path-data 'drop-in' seed was wrong, but one specific mechanism cited for the graft cost (hand-placed node positions) is overstated since positions auto-compute by default.
  - unsupported: "every upstream technology and lathe recipe would need re-slotting into their layout and hand-placed node positions" — TechnologyPrototype.cs (upstream Content.Shared/Research/Prototypes/) shows Position is an *optional* override with the comment "Optional manual position override for the fancy console menu. When unset, positions are computed automatically." (marked 'backmen: rnd-auto-layout'). So the tree does NOT require hand-placing node positions for every technology; auto-layout is the actual default, which undercuts the specific 'hand-placed node positions' re-slotting cost cited in skip_because.

**goobstation**

*loop-change · needs upstream edits · medium confidence · 6 forks carry it*

The research console stops being a flat list and becomes a map you drag around and zoom in and out of, with every technology sitting as a card connected to its prerequisites; locked tech you have not qualified for is hidden behind TV static, and a "Recenter" button snaps you back if you get lost. Clicking a card shows its point cost, its prerequisites, and picture cards of every recipe it will unlock, plus a percentage showing how far through that tier the station is, and a toggle to show only what has already been researched. The tree itself is much bigger than upstream's: scientists can chase mech chassis lines (Ripley MK-II, Clarke, and Gygax/Durand which need CentComm to sign off), MOD suits, energy-cell pistols/SMGs/snipers/LMGs, bananium weapons, plumbing, cloning, xenobiology gear and bluespace kit, and lathes announce "database has been updated with N new recipes" as each unlock lands, with recipes sorted into new fabricator categories per mech and suit line.

- **Take** — The pannable prerequisite-graph console with static-fogged locked nodes and recipe preview cards is a large, immediately legible upgrade over upstream's flat technology list, and it makes a long research tree readable instead of overwhelming.
- **Skip** — The console UI is only half of it: most of the technologies and lathe packs unlock Goob-specific content (mech chassis lines, MOD suits, biofab synthetic organs, energy-cell gun families), so taking the tree wholesale drags in several other fork systems, and taking only the UI means re-authoring the node graph against your own content and re-checking node positions every time you add tech.
- **Touches** — science, engineering, medical, cargo, security, command
- **Needs** — [mech-overhaul](#mech-overhaul), [modular-hardsuits](#modular-hardsuits)
- **Verified** — partly supported. The claim's UI description is largely correct — I directly confirmed pan/zoom/drag (MinZoom 0.5/MaxZoom 2, mouse-drag repositioning), the Recenter button, prerequisite connector lines (ResearchesContainerPanel.Draw), per-card cost/prereq/recipe-unlock info panels with picture cards (MiniRecipeCardControl showing Showcase.Texture), tier-percentage display, the lathe "database has been updated with N new recipes" message, and the large Goob-specific tech list (Ripley MK-II/Clarke/Gygax/Durand-with-CentComm, MOD suits, energy-cell gun families, bananium weapons, plumbing, xenobiology, bluespace, cloning). But two specific UI claims are unsupported: nothing hides locked tech behind static (all techs are always sent and just color-coded red when Unavailable), and no "researched-only" toggle exists anywhere in the client files. On graft shape, the claim already downgraded the seed's 'drop-in' guess to 'needs-upstream-edits', and I found direct proof this is correct in the strongest sense: the fork's own tree contains edited copies of genuinely upstream files — Content.Shared/Research/Prototypes/TechnologyPrototype.cs (adds a required Position field with a "Goobstation R&D console rework" comment), Content.Shared/Research/Components/SharedResearchConsoleComponent.cs (adds a Researches dictionary to the BUI state), and Content.Server/Research/Systems/ResearchSystem.Console.cs (rewrites UpdateConsoleInterface with old logic commented out as "goob - rework"). This is fork-patches-upstream, not merely integration-would-require-edits — the edits already exist in the fork's own commit history.
  - unsupported: "locked tech you have not qualified for is hidden behind TV static" — ResearchSystem.Console.cs builds techList from ALL TechnologyPrototypes with no Hidden-field or Unavailable filtering, and FancyResearchConsoleItem.xaml.cs renders every tech as a visible card (Unavailable techs get DarkRed/Crimson coloring, not concealment). The 'rnd-static.rsi' AnimatedTextureRect is a single cosmetic background layer behind the whole DragContainer panel, not a per-node lock overlay.
  - unsupported: "a toggle to show only what has already been researched" — no checkbox/toggle/filter control exists anywhere in FancyResearchConsoleMenu.xaml(.cs), FancyResearchConsoleItem, FancyTechnologyInfoPanel, or ResearchesContainerPanel; searched all client UI files for toggle/checkbox/filter/onlyresearched with no hits.

**far-horizons**

*loop-change · needs upstream edits · high confidence · 6 forks carry it*

Science works from a visual, searchable tech map instead of the stock discipline console: nodes sit in three tiers, each with an icon, a point cost and prerequisite lines to earlier nodes, and you pick one and click Research to see a progress bar fill toward its cost. Points collect in a station bank that has a hard ceiling and bleeds away once full, so the console nags over the radio that the bank is maxed and someone needs to queue work; scientists line up to three technologies in a queue (more once queue-size upgrades are bought), and every queue add, removal and completed unlock is broadcast on the radio with the approver's name. Alongside the usual lathe recipes, some nodes hand out station-wide perks rather than items, such as unlocking plastic surgery, making surgery faster, or raising the point bank and queue limits, and higher tiers only open after the station has banked enough total research.

- **Take** — It turns research from a menu of purchases into a visible map with pacing pressure, a bank that punishes idling and radio chatter that makes science's progress legible to the whole station.
- **Skip** — It replaces the research console wholesale, so every lathe recipe's tech gating has to be re-mapped onto the new node graph, and the shipped tree assumes fork content (shuttle guns, mechs, cyberlimbs, bananium weapons) plus a vendored Starlight discipline set you would have to prune or reproduce.
- **Touches** — science, engineering, medical, security, cargo, command
- **Verified** — partly supported. Fetched all 10 cited files plus the actual C# systems (not cited, but decisive): Content.Server/_FarHorizons/Research/ResearchSystem.{cs,Tree.cs,Console.cs} is a self-contained new FHResearchSystem, but it calls _research.RemoveLatheRecipe(), which is defined inside Content.Shared/Research/Systems/SharedResearchSystem.cs — an upstream-owned file with no _FarHorizons segment — under a literal "// Far Horizons start" marker (confirmed against upstream space-wizards/space-station-14's version of the same file, which has AddLatheRecipe but not RemoveLatheRecipe). That is a real in-place upstream edit the path-data heuristic couldn't see, so fork-patches-upstream is directly confirmed. Separately, the console wholesale-replaces the stock research UI and layers on top of upstream TechnologyDatabaseComponent/ResearchServerComponent, so wiring it into another codebase (honksquad-ss14) would itself require touching that codebase's own copy of SharedResearchSystem.cs and re-mapping every lathe recipe onto the new node graph — integration-would-require-upstream-edits also holds. Both readings are true simultaneously, which is why "both" applies.
  - unsupported: "every queue add, removal and completed unlock is broadcast on the radio with the approver's name" — the completed-unlock broadcast (research-tree-unlock-broadcast = "Unlocked {$technology} for {$amount} research.") carries only the technology name and point amount, no approver field. Only the queue-add and queue-remove broadcasts (research-tree-console-add-queue-radio-broadcast / -remove-queue-radio-broadcast) include the approver's identity.

**monolith**

*loop-change · entangled · high confidence · 6 forks carry it*

Research stops being one science tree and becomes a set of rival manufacturer catalogues: you first buy a shared spine of tiered "Material Research" and "Ballistics Research" nodes, then branch into a corporation or faction you want to arm yourself from, each with its own T1-T3 ladder priced in the tens of thousands of points. Mieyo sells breaching gear, wound treatment and bionics; the pirate PDV branch sells ballistics, thermal imaging, a portable hacking tool and blood-red imitation suits; other branches sell energy weapons, hardsuits, mechs, drones, and warship munitions like torpedoes, railgun shells and fighter ordnance. Several nodes unlock shipyard vouchers by grade rather than an item, so researching far enough is how a crew earns the right to buy bigger ships. A second console turns stored research points back into physical 1k, 5k and 10k data disks after a short print cycle, so points become objects you can pocket, hand to another crew or feed into building "data farm" machines instead of only spending them at your own lathe.

- **Take** — The point-disk printer is the genuinely portable idea here: making research points into a physical, printable, tradeable disk turns science output into something crews can carry, trade and steal instead of a number locked to one server.
- **Skip** — The tree itself is written for Monolith's multi-ship sector setting, with nodes whose payload is faction-branded gear, ship vouchers and torpedo ammunition that do not exist on a station fork, so grafting the disciplines means importing or reinventing hundreds of entity prototypes before a single node unlocks anything.
- **Touches** — science, engineering, cargo, security, medical, command, all-players
- **Needs** — [shipyard-player-ships](#shipyard-player-ships), [ship-to-ship-combat](#ship-to-ship-combat)
- **Verified** — supported. Every specific gameplay claim I checked matched a real file: Material/Ballistics Research spine (prerequisites.ftl), per-faction disciplines Mieyo/RogueShipyard/RogueGear/RogueWeaponry/Ullman/TSF/USSP (disciplines + Organizations dir listing), Mieyo's breaching gear/wound treatment/bionics (mieyo.yml technology prototypes with recipeUnlocks HyposprayMMC, AccessBreakerMMC, AutosurgeonSandevistanMMC), PDV's ballistics/thermal/hacking/blood-red suits (rogue-research.ftl technology names), tiered shipyard-voucher unlocks (rogue_misc.yml PdvTierOneVouchers/TwoVouchers/ThreeVouchers with recipeUnlocks like ShipVoucherPdvT0Recipe, costs 40000-80000), and the 1k/5k/10k point-disk printer with a print-duration timer feeding a DataFarm machine board that literally requires 2x ResearchDisk10000 as a build tag (SharedPointDiskConsole.cs, PointDiskConsoleSystem.cs, datafarms.yml). On graft_shape, I confirm entangled and go further than the claim itself: the fork doesn't just add new _Mono files, it directly edits upstream Resources/Prototypes/Research/arsenal.yml (and sibling disciplines.yml/civilianservices.yml/industrial.yml), commenting out original techs under "Mono edit - research consolidation" headers — none of which appear in the cited evidence list. Content.Server/_Mono also has separate Shipyard/Ships/SpaceArtillery/Weapons directories, corroborating the stated depends_on (shipyard-player-ships, ship-to-ship-combat). This unit is entangled by every measure, not a drop-in.
  - unsupported: "priced in the tens of thousands of points" — true for most nodes (10k-125k) but MieyoMedicalGear (Wound Treatment) is 5000 points, below "tens of thousands"

### Construction and crafting

<a id="construction-and-crafting"></a>

Multi-step construction graphs for walls, machines and furniture plus hand-crafting recipes and rapid construction devices.

**corvax, cosmatic-drift, ephemeral-space, funky, gaby-station-now-dumont-station, goobstation, impstation, monolith, rmc14, serbia-strong**

*activity · needs upstream edits · medium confidence · 12 forks carry it*

Across these ten forks this is mostly a large pile of extra things you can build and print: park benches, pews and sofas you place tile by tile, boarded-up windows, spider-web nests, secure trash bins, wall-mounted computers, crates and cardboard boxes, food you assemble by hand (steaks, candy), and lathe menus stocked with fork-specific clothing, ammo, tiles and even printed paperwork forms sorted into categories like "Complaints" and "Orders". A few forks go past recipes into new engineering behaviour: on one, walls and machines no longer just shatter but turn into a "broken" version that examines as repairable with a named tool, so you patch damage instead of rebuilding from sheets; on another, a charged repair tool rebuilds destroyed pieces of a ship back onto ghostly outlines of where they used to be; the marine fork gives its frontline technician a dedicated build menu for throwing up sandbag lines, barbed wire and barricades under fire and then upgrading them in place. Smaller touches include inflatable emergency walls and doors printed from durathread, flatpacks you drop and unfold into a working machine, and upgrade kits that bump an installed machine to a better tier without deconstructing it.

- **Take** — The recipe and lathe portion is pure content: it gives engineers, cargo and service crew more to build during quiet stretches without touching how any existing job is played.
- **Skip** — It is not one feature but ten unrelated fork content dumps, and the genuinely interesting parts (breakable-instead-of-destroyed walls, ship repair ghosts, field fortification building) each drag in their own systems and their own art, so you end up cherry-picking anyway and maintaining recipes that reference entities you may not have.
- **Touches** — engineering, cargo, service, security, science, all-players
- **Verified** — partly supported. Re-fetched all 11 cited evidence files and they back the core mechanics well: ES's breakable.ftl literally reads "It's broken. It can be repaired using a {$tool}", Monolith's ship-repair/tool.ftl names a "repair ghost" entity and charge-based failure strings matching the claimed ghost-outline repair tool, RMC's Combat Technician guidebook page describes sandbags, barbed-wire lacing, and in-place metal/plasteel/MB-6 barricade upgrades in exactly the detail claimed, CD's furniture.yml lists BenchPark*, BenchPew*, RattySofa*/CorpSofa* construction recipes (park benches, pews, sofas confirmed), Funky's inflatables.yml prints InflatableWall/InflatableDoor from Durathread, and corvax's lathe-categories.ftl contains literal "Complaints" and "Orders" categories. That part of the claim is solid. But several illustrative specifics in the prose — boarded-up windows, spider-web nests, secure trash bins, wall-mounted computers, crates/cardboard boxes, hand-assembled steak/candy food, flatpacks, and machine upgrade kits — appear nowhere in the 11 cited files, so I could not verify them; they may exist elsewhere in these large forks but the claim states them as if directly evidenced. On graft_shape: I traced Funky's InflatableWall recipe into Resources/Prototypes/Entities/Structures/Machines/lathe.yml — the vanilla (non-namespaced) file defining the base Autolathe — and found the fork has directly inserted "- InflatableWall #funky inflatables" and several other "#funk"-tagged lines into that shared file's staticRecipes list, alongside pre-existing "Delta-V additions" markers from other forks. This proves the fork's own tree edits an upstream-path file in place (fork-patches-upstream), and separately, wiring any of these lathe recipes into another codebase would require editing that codebase's own lathe/autolathe recipe list too (integration-would-require-upstream-edits) — both readings hold. This directly refutes the "drop-in" seed and confirms the assessor's "needs-upstream-edits" call.

### Power grid and device networking

<a id="power-grid-and-device-networking"></a>

Cable-based power distribution with APCs, SMES units, substations and generators, plus wired and wireless device networks with link configurators. A console is only here if it reads or controls power or the device network; consoles that merely happen to be machines are `device-and-machine-additions`.

**rmc14**

*structural · entangled · medium confidence · 5 forks carry it*

Power here is not a web of wires you trace with a multitool, it is a handful of big fusion reactors feeding rooms directly. Engineers keep the reactors fed with fusion fuel cells (a slow ten-second swap), and patch broken ones back together through a wrench-then-wire-then-weld repair sequence while the reactor's face shows how much juice is left. Every room has its own APC with a battery, a main breaker, a charge toggle and three separate switches for equipment, lighting and environment, each set to auto, forced on, or forced off; it is ID-locked and screwdriver-locked, and a marine without real engineering training cannot do anything with it beyond stare at the screen. The sabotage side is the drama: someone can rig a reactor to overload, at which point it starts humming and hissing warnings at anyone nearby, and an engineer with a multitool has to get there and shut it back down before the lights go out. Bulbs and tubes are physical objects that shatter when something hits them, burn your bare hand if you grab them, and simply die when the reactors do, so losing power means fighting in the dark.

- **Take** — It turns power from background plumbing into a defendable objective: a small number of reactors that can be fed, broken, repaired and sabotaged, with room-by-room APC control and lights that actually go out when the reactors do.
- **Skip** — It replaces the upstream cable-and-node power grid wholesale rather than sitting beside it, so every powered machine, every map area and every APC on your stations has to be converted; on top of that the APC and reactor interactions are hard-gated behind RMC's engineer skill levels and its own access-level ids, and the overload path assumes a xeno-style antagonist exists to trigger it.
- **Touches** — engineering, antagonist, command, all-players
- **Needs** — [squads-ranks-and-skills](#squads-ranks-and-skills), [access-control-rework](#access-control-rework)
- **Verified** — supported. Every specific gameplay beat checks out against real code: fusion reactor Watts/CellDelay=10s/CellRemoveDelay=10s do-afters, Wrench→Wire→Weld RMCFusionReactorState repair sequence, charge-level visual enum (Ten/TwentyFive/.../Overloaded/Empty), RMCApcComponent's MainBreakerButton/ChargeModeButton/three Equipment-Lighting-Environment channels each with Auto/On/Off RMCApcButtonState, Locked+Access=[CMAccessEngineering,...]+RepairTool=Screwing gating, and OverloadQuality=\"Pulsing\" matching the vanilla Multitool's own Tool quality (confirmed in Resources/Prototypes/Entities/Objects/Tools/tools.yml) plus OverloadHumSound/OverloadHissSound. Light bulbs/tubes shatter via Destructible+DamageOnLand/DamageOtherOnHit in light_bulb.yml; the \"burns your hand\" behavior is real but lives in upstream Content.Server/Light/EntitySystems/PoweredLightSystem.cs (inherited vanilla behavior, not fork code — doesn't contradict the claim, just clarifies provenance). On graft_shape: the claim already downgraded the seed's naive \"drop-in\" to \"entangled\", and that downgrade is correct. RMCApcComponent and RMCFusionReactorComponent hard-depend on Content.Shared._RMC14.Marines.Skills (RMCSkillEngineer/SkillLevel) and RMC-specific AccessLevelPrototype ids (CMAccessEngineering/CMAccessColonyEngineering) — both separate fork subsystems, not upstream. SharedRMCPowerSystem.cs also imports Content.Shared._RMC14.Xenonids, confirming the overload path's antagonist dependency. Architecturally the fork disables the vanilla wire network at the root (coil.yml's CablePlacer component is literally commented out) while still reaching into vanilla SharedApcPowerReceiverComponent/SharedPowerReceiverSystem to flip .Powered directly — a genuine wholesale swap of the distribution layer, not a bolt-on. All of this is self-contained under _RMC14 namespaced files/directories (no upstream file edits found), so it would import cleanly, but it is functionally entangled with two other fork-specific systems (skills, access) and one antagonist system (xenonids), matching the claim's own \"entangled\" label rather than the seed's \"drop-in\" guess.

**ephemeral-space**

*loop-change · needs upstream edits · medium confidence · 5 forks carry it*

Engineering's main power source is an antimatter engine: instead of a machine you tune, the antimatter is a pool sitting in a containment area that literally grows when it is fed plasma gas, creeps onto neighbouring tiles once it gets too big, eats anything that touches it with a nasty radiation-pulse crackle, and detonates if it is allowed to grow past its limit. Converter machines placed around it siphon a little of that mass off every few seconds and turn it into electricity for the grid, and a converter that takes damage stops working until someone welds it back together (examining it says the accumulator is broken). The fork also writes a proper set of in-game power guides that teach players to read a Power Monitoring Computer, multitool a cable to see supply versus demand on that specific voltage network, understand why generators ramp up slowly and cause brownouts, and set up PACMAN portable generators, plus a few small device-linking additions (keypads that fire "unlock" and "lock" signals to whatever you wire them to, and shared radio frequencies for armory, radstorm and warp-drive countdown timers).

- **Take** — It turns setting up the station engine into a live containment problem (feed it, fence it in, drain it) rather than a start-it-and-forget-it machine, and the power guidebook pages are genuinely useful teaching material regardless of which engine you run.
- **Skip** — The antimatter guidebook page is an unwritten "TODO write the rest lol" stub, so you would be porting an engine with no player-facing documentation and would have to author the containment room, converter placement and station mapping yourself before anyone can use it.
- **Touches** — engineering, atmospherics, all-players
- **Verified** — supported. Every substantive gameplay claim checks out against the actual source: ESAntimatterComponent grows via GrowthGas=Plasma consumed from the tile atmosphere (OnDeviceUpdate), spreads to neighbor tiles once Mass>OverflowMass (ActiveEdgeSpreaderComponent + OnSpreadNeighbors), detonates via _explosion.TriggerExplosive when Mass>ExplosionMassAmount and can't spread further, and consumes touching entities via OnEntityConsumed (EventHorizon) while playing a RadiationPulse sound collection. ESAntimatterConverterComponent.Broken is set by a standard BreakageEventArgs (damage) and cleared by RepairedEvent (welding), with an examine line 'The accumulator is broken!' matching exactly. The Update loop drains RemovalAmount mass every ~1s into battery charge at EnergyPerMass W/mass — matches 'siphon mass off every few seconds' into electricity. All five guidebook pages read verbatim match the claim's description, including the AME.xml stub being literally '# TODO ES write the rest Lol'. The device-linking additions (ESKeypadUnlock/Lock source ports, Armory/Radstorm/WarpDrive timer frequencies) are exact prototype/locale matches. On graft shape: every file found (Content.Server/_ES, Content.Shared/_ES, Content.Client/_ES, Resources/Prototypes/_ES, Resources/Locale/_ES, Resources/ServerInfo/_ES) lives in the fork's own _ES namespace — the fork's copy does not patch upstream files. The claim's needs-upstream-edits verdict is about wiring cost (placing the containment room/converters on a target station map), not about the source fork itself touching upstream directories, so it correctly reads as integration-would-require-upstream-edits rather than fork-patches-upstream.

**starlight**

*loop-change · needs upstream edits · medium confidence · 5 forks carry it*

Engineering gets a bluespace harvester: a machine you dial up through ten levels, each one eating exponentially more power (1 kW at level 1, 100 MW at level 10) and paying out points you spend on randomised loot crates. Push it past level 7 and it starts tearing open portals beside itself that dump two to five hostile creatures onto the deck and lock the machine out until the mess is cleared, so the profitable settings are the ones that bite back. Separately, docking a shuttle to the station now welds the two high-voltage cable grids together automatically, so a ship can feed off station power or power the station while docked, and atmos devices (filters, mixers, pressure and volume pumps, injectors) can be wired to buttons and sensors so a tech can flip or retune a whole gas setup remotely instead of clicking each machine. Smaller additions round it out: lockers that need power and can be hacked open or electrified through a wire panel, signal ports for scan gates, mass drivers, ticket machines, body scanners and turret banks, and batteries that trickle-charge themselves.

- **Take** — The bluespace harvester is a genuine risk/reward power sink that gives engineering a reason to overbuild the grid, and cable-over-dock quietly fixes the long-standing awkwardness of powering a docked shuttle.
- **Skip** — It is three unrelated features sharing a folder — the harvester needs its own hostile mobs, portal entity and loot-pool prototypes to come with it, the atmos signal work has to be attached to upstream gas-device prototypes device by device, and the cable-docking system reaches into upstream node-group internals plus three fork CCVars, so none of it lands as a clean copy.
- **Touches** — engineering, atmospherics, cargo, security, service, medical, shuttle-crew
- **Verified** — partly supported. The claim's own downgrade from the drop-in seed to needs-upstream-edits holds up, and more strongly than the claim argues: the fork's own binary.yml/trinary.yml/unary.yml (upstream-namespace atmos device prototypes, not under _Starlight) already contain inline '# Starlight start' / '# Starlight end' edit blocks adding DeviceLinkSink ports directly into those upstream files - that is fork-patches-upstream, not merely a hypothetical wiring step for a future integrator. Meanwhile CableDockingSystem.cs and the BluespaceHarvester files are genuinely self-contained under _Starlight/, only consuming pre-existing public upstream APIs (DockEvent/UndockEvent, CableNode.AddAlwaysReachable/QueueReflood) without altering upstream files, so that half of the unit fits the 'would need upstream edits to wire in elsewhere' reading instead. Both patterns coexist in this one unit.
  - unsupported: "batteries that trickle-charge themselves" — no cited evidence file mentions batteries at all, and a directory listing of Content.Server/_Starlight/Power found no battery-related file; this detail is unverified.
  - unsupported: "it starts tearing open portals beside itself that dump two to five hostile creatures onto the deck and lock the machine out until the mess is cleared" — the mob-count range (2-5) and level-7 threshold are exactly confirmed in BluespaceHarvesterComponent.cs, but the unlock mechanism is only confirmed to be 'portal entity ComponentShutdown' (BluespaceHarvesterSystem.cs OnPortalShutdown); whether that shutdown is gated on killing the spawned mobs versus a plain timer (PortalBlockDuration=30f is declared on the component but never referenced in the system file, and the portal's own entity-prototype/despawn logic was not located) was not confirmed, so 'until the mess is cleared' implying required player action may overstate it.

### Shuttle piloting and navigation extensions

<a id="shuttle-piloting-extensions"></a>

Adds autopilot, boost modes, scuttling, radar blips, docking rules and scheduled transit routes on top of manual shuttle flight.

**corvax, frontier, monolith, rmc14, serbia-strong, starlight**

*loop-change · needs upstream edits · high confidence · 8 forks carry it*

A pilot sitting at a shuttle console gets a lot more than thrust and rotation. They can flip the engines between Cruise (drift freely), Drive (dampened, stops when you let go) and Park (locked in place), drop a marked waypoint on the radar and steer to it, search nearby contacts by IFF name, undock every airlock at once with one button, and on some forks hand the helm to an autopilot that flies to the chosen destination and pops "Autopilot Arrived" when it gets there. Ships can advertise what they are offering to everyone else's radar with little icons (music note for services aboard, dollar for a shop, smiley for a hangout), docking ports get readable names like "1A", "CB2" or "McDrive Thru" so traffic control can talk people in, and a stealth console lets a ship drop off IFF entirely for a timed window before going on cooldown. Crew without a ship of their own can read a bus timetable that tells them which numbered route is running, which bus is coming and how long until it reaches each station, then ride an NPC-scheduled shuttle between destinations. Ships also gain a self-destruct: someone arms an antimatter scuttle charge, a station-wide announcement names the ship and counts down the seconds, and anyone who can reach the device in time can spend a long fiddly do-after disarming it. RMC-14's slice is a different game entirely: crewed dropships that fly troops to a landing zone and run close air support, with fabricated cannons, guided missiles and napalm rockets, engine modules that cut refuel and travel time, and medevac and fulton mounts for pulling casualties off the ground.

- **Take** — The console-side pieces (cruise/drive/park modes, radar waypoints, IFF search, undock-all, named dock labels) are small quality-of-life wins that make flying a shuttle legible instead of a wrestling match, and they are useful on any map that has more than one destination.
- **Skip** — Every fork's version hooks into the upstream shuttle console UI and ShuttleConsoleSystem as partials/overrides, so this rides directly on the part of upstream that churns most; the genuinely exciting bits (public transit routes, dropship CAS) only pay off if you already have a multi-destination sector or a whole marine gamemode to hang them on.
- **Touches** — engineering, command, cargo, service, all-players
- **Needs** — [ruins-poi-and-sector-generation](#ruins-poi-and-sector-generation)
- **Verified** — partly supported. I fetched all cited .ftl/.xml/.yml/.cs files and they back the specific mechanics named: Frontier's console.ftl has the exact Cruise/Drive/Park labels, radar target/waypoint strings, IFF search, undock-all; dock.ftl has 1A/CB2/McDrive Thru style labels; bus-schedule ftl + public_transit_routes.yml confirm numbered routes and arrival-time strings; Monolith's console.ftl has the Autopilot button and "Autopilot Arrived" popup; Monolith's scuttle-device.ftl confirms the antimatter self-destruct with named-location countdown announcement and a fiddly disarm warning; ss220's computer-iff-ebent-console.ftl confirms the stealth/cooldown console; RMC-14's CAS guide confirms guided missiles, napalm rockets (7x7 fire), fulton recovery, and medevac stretcher mounts. I also fetched the actual upstream-path Content.Server/Shuttles/Systems/ShuttleConsoleSystem.cs from Frontier, Monolith, SS220 and Starlight and found it directly edited in place with inline fork-tagged comments (// Frontier, _Mono usings, // SS220, // Starlight) rather than untouched with new sibling files, which affirmatively confirms the claim's downgrade from the seed's drop-in guess to needs-upstream-edits, and settles upstream_reading as fork-patches-upstream (the forks' own copies genuinely contain edited upstream-path files) while integration would also require upstream edits to wire in elsewhere, so both readings hold. The one real gap: Corvax (space-syndicate/space-station-14) is named as one of the six forks in the unit, but no evidence was cited for it and my own check of its ShuttleConsoleSystem.cs shows zero Corvax-specific markers and none of cruise/dampen/autopilot/IFF logic, so its inclusion in this bundle is unsupported by anything I could find.
  - unsupported: Listing 'corvax' as one of the six forks contributing to this feature set — no path was cited for it and a direct check of Corvax's Content.Server/Shuttles/Systems/ShuttleConsoleSystem.cs shows no Corvax-specific markers and no cruise/dampen/autopilot/IFF-search code, so the claim's fork list overstates which forks actually carry these mechanics.

### Supermatter engine

<a id="supermatter-engine"></a>

A crystal power source that converts gas and matter into enormous power and delaminates catastrophically when mismanaged, with its own monitoring console and warning audio.

**serbia-strong**

*structural · needs upstream edits · high confidence · 5 forks carry it*

Engineering gets a giant crystal as an alternative station power source, and babysitting it is a full-time job. The crystal ships inert; hitting it with an object or a shot wakes it up, after which it eats the gas around it, throws lightning arcs into tesla coils and radiation into collectors, and belches out superheated oxygen and plasma that has to be cooled and filtered by a chamber the engineers build themselves (no map ships a ready-made one). Engineers feed it matter and energy with dedicated supermatter emitters they tune by hand, and watch its integrity, internal energy, matter, temperature and per-gas effects on a monitoring console or on a PDA app anyone can install. Standing near it without meson goggles and rad protection gives you hallucinations and radiation sickness. Let its energy drift outside the safe band and integrity bleeds away: engineering radio warns first, then the whole station is told, then Central Command hears the delamination countdown, and if nobody drags it back in time the crystal explodes, or turns into a singularity or a tesla ball that starts eating the station.

- **Take** — It is the single richest engineering minigame in SS13 that upstream SS14 lacks: a permanent, multi-person job for the engineering department whose failure state is a station-wide catastrophe the whole crew has to react to.
- **Skip** — It is a ~100-file simulation (thermodynamics, per-gas response curves, integrity, delamination variants, its own emitter, console, cartridge, hardsuit and audio) that only pays off if you also commit to map work, containment-chamber design and balance tuning; a badly ported version either never delaminates or delaminates every round.
- **Touches** — engineering, atmospherics, command, all-players
- **Verified** — supported. Directly cloned the fork's tree (git ls-tree) and confirmed all ~121 SuperMatter/SuperMatterEmitter/Observer/Cartridge .cs and .yml files live under SS220/ namespace dirs, matching the drop-in path-data signal. But content-grepping non-namespace files (something path data cannot do) found the fork editing three genuinely upstream files in place: Resources/Prototypes/Guidebook/engineering.yml (adds \"- Supermatter # SS220-superMatter-crystal\" to the vanilla guide-category list), Resources/Prototypes/Research/industrial.yml, and Resources/Prototypes/Recipes/Lathes/Packs/engineering.yml (both add \"SuperMatterObserverCircuitboard # SS220 superMatter-crystal\" to vanilla tech-unlock/lathe-recipe lists). These are real edits to upstream files carrying SS220 comment tags, not new files, so this is fork-patches-upstream, not merely integration-would-require-upstream-edits. The gameplay description itself checks out almost line-for-line against the Russian guidebook text and the crystal.yml/UI-state code (inert-until-hit activation, gas consumption, LightningArcShooter/RadiationSource output to tesla coils/collectors, hot O2+plasma byproduct with \"NT currently has no standard containment chamber\" text matching \"no map ships a ready-made one,\" SuperMatterObserverUpdateState exposing integrity/energy/matter/temperature/per-gas ratios, freely-installable Cartridge-type PDA app, and the three-stage engineering-radio to station-wide to CentCom delamination warning sequence verbatim in the guidebook, ending in Explosive/Singularity/TeslaEnergyBall outcomes).
  - unsupported: "Standing near it without meson goggles and rad protection gives you hallucinations and radiation sickness" — the guidebook and crystal.yml only show a generic `EyeProtection` component check (satisfied by any eye-protection item, e.g. "engineering goggles") plus a bare `RadiationSource`; no file names a specific "meson goggles" or "rad protection" item, so the general mechanic is right but the specific gear names are the claim author's gloss, not something the evidence states.

**einstein-engines**

*structural · needs upstream edits · high confidence · 5 forks carry it*

Engineering gets a glowing crystal that eats the gas around it and turns it into station power, and it talks back: it announces its own integrity over the radio, growls and hums louder as it heats up, and screams "Crystal hyperstructure integrity faltering!" when engineers let the gas mix go wrong. A monitoring console shows live integrity, internal energy in eV, radiation output, absorbed moles, temperature versus its limit, waste multiplier and per-gas breakdown, with a status readout climbing from Normal through Caution, Warning, Danger, Emergency to Delaminating. Anyone who walks into it is flashed into a pile of ash, a saboteur can carve a sliver off the crystal (which halves the delamination timer and triggers a Central Command announcement blaming Engineering), and if nobody saves it the countdown runs out and it delaminates into a station-wrecking explosion, a singularity, a tesla ball, or an unstoppable resonance cascade depending on how it died.

- **Take** — It is the one engine that makes power generation an ongoing, tense job rather than a setup task: it degrades on its own, it announces its own decline to the whole station, and a bad shift ends the round, so Engineering has a reason to stay at their post all round.
- **Skip** — It is a large, tightly-coupled simulation (98 files, its own console UI, hundreds of audio clips, sliver/kudzu/lightning/singularity/tesla spawn chains) whose difficulty curve is tuned against Einstein Engines' atmos and map layouts, so grafting it means owning a balance surface you will be retuning for months, and its prototype also carries EE's LanguageSpeaker/LanguageKnowledge components that must be stripped or ported.
- **Touches** — engineering, atmospherics, science, antagonist, command, all-players
- **Verified** — supported. *structural · entangled · high confidence · 5 forks carry it*
