### Fusion reactor

<a id="fusion-reactor"></a>

A multi-part fusion engine fed by fuel and moderator gases through a control console, with fuel rods, tuners and its own catalogue of failure modes.

**stellar-station**

*loop-change · entangled · high confidence · 1 forks carry it*

Instead of a singularity or supermatter, engineering runs a multi-tile "Stellarator": you feed a coloured fuel rod (plasma, uranium, supermatter or the volatile echion) into a hatch on the front of the reactor, and then crew have to physically stand on contact pads on the two tuning modules flanking it and keep re-tuning them, because each tuner's calibration constantly drifts out of the green ("The tuner's Calibration shifts!") and a screen on each module shows green/yellow/red. Hold both tuners calibrated long enough and the core visibly charges up and the station gets a broadcast overcharge matching the rod you burned - offensive, defensive, curative or scientific - with a short guaranteed grace period before upkeep resumes, and the exotic rods can push a second tier of hypercharge. Let it slide and the reactor starts throwing hazards at the room: tuners overload and need welding back, vents blow gas, fires start, and the cable clusters running out of the engine electrify and shock or fling anyone caught standing on them.

- **Take** — It turns the station engine from a set-and-forget power source into an ongoing two-person babysitting minigame with a station-wide reward attached, which is a genuinely different shape from singularity/supermatter/AME.
- **Skip** — It is visibly mid-development in the source fork (fuel rods still say "LOREM IPSUM", one popup is marked PLACEHOLDER, the grace timers are debug-shortened to 10s) and the engine is only half the feature - the overcharge buffs it exists to grant are a separate fork system you would have to port and balance yourself, on top of finding map room for the multi-tile assembly.
- **Touches** — engineering, atmospherics, security, medical, science, all-players
- **Needs** — [shared-utility-libraries](#shared-utility-libraries), [custom-station-maps](#custom-station-maps)
- **Verified** — supported. All six cited files were fetched and read in full. Nearly every specific detail in the gameplay description checks out verbatim: stellarator.ftl has "The tuner's Calibration shifts!" and the exact "# PLACEHOLDER" comment on the tuner-broken popup; fuelrods.yml has literal "description: LOREM IPSUM" on the plasma and uranium rods and maps plasma->Scientific, uranium->Curative, supermatter->Defensive, echion->Offensive overcharge, with canHypercharge:true only on the two "exotic" rods (supermatter, echion); StellarEngineCoreComponent.cs has GracePeriodOvercharged/Hypercharged both hard-set to TimeSpan.FromSeconds(10f) with commented-out original values (//90f, //150f) confirming the "debug-shortened to 10s" claim exactly; StellarEngineTunerSystem.cs shows the DoAfter-based re-tuning loop, calibration decay/wiggle-buildup mechanic, green/yellow/red state thresholds, BreakTuner+Weldable repair flow, and engine.yml shows the multi-tile layout (core, fuel-input, left/right tuners with contact pads, electrified cable-cluster entity with Shock/Heat damage and throw), matching "vents blow gas, fires start, cables electrify and fling." On graft_shape: the claim already self-downgraded the seed's "drop-in" guess to "entangled," and the code supports that downgrade — StellarEngineTunerSystem.cs pulls in Content.Shared._ES.Sparks (ESSparksSystem) and an AudioHelpers pitch-shift utility that live outside this unit's own Stellarator files, i.e. genuine dependencies on other fork subsystems, not upstream-file edits. So I concur with entangled over drop-in.
  - unsupported: "fuel rods still say \"LOREM IPSUM\"" is stated as a general fact about the fuel rods, but only 2 of the 4 fetched fuel-rod prototypes (plasma, uranium) actually have that placeholder description — supermatter and echion have real flavor text ("Contains a core made of Hyperdense Crystalline Substrate...", "Houses a volume of 'Echion'..."). Minor generalization, not a fabrication.

**funky**

*activity · entangled · high confidence · 1 forks carry it*

Engineering can order a crate of flatpacked reactor parts and bolt together a nine-tile fusion machine on the floor: a glowing core in the middle, four corners, and three edge pieces you choose the placement of for fuel intake, moderator intake and waste output. At the console you pick a fuel pairing (tritium/hydrogen, plasma/oxygen, hypernoblium/antinoblium and others), set injection rates in moles per second, and then babysit four dials (heating conductor, cooling volume, magnetic constrictor, current damper) while watching fusion level, energy, reaction activity and instability climb. Run it well and it churns out exotic gases you cannot easily make anywhere else; run it badly and it eats 100 kW, starts screaming warnings, pulses radiation and tugs at nearby objects, and eventually melts down with an explosion, EMP and a spreading gas disaster whose severity depends on which fuel you chose. It cannot be switched off or unbolted while the reaction is still hot, so a bad start is something the crew has to talk down rather than walk away from.

- **Take** — It gives atmos a genuine second endgame project with a real failure state: a multi-tile machine you assemble yourself, eight fuel recipes with different risk profiles, and a meltdown that is dramatic without being an instant round-ender, all wired to a purpose-built console rather than a single interact verb.
- **Skip** — Every fuel recipe is written against gases upstream SS14 does not have (hydrogen, helium, hypernoblium, antinoblium, BZ, pluoxium, halon, zauker, healium, proto-nitrate, nitrium), so the reactor is useless without first grafting an exotic-gas expansion and the atmos plumbing to produce those gases; the machine also produces no power, so its entire payoff is downstream gas content you would have to want anyway.
- **Touches** — engineering, atmospherics, cargo
- **Needs** — [exotic-gas-expansion](#exotic-gas-expansion), [atmospherics-simulation](#atmospherics-simulation)
- **Verified** — partly supported. The core mechanics check out against the cited files: hfr.yml defines fusionRecipe entries pairing gases (Plasma+Oxygen, Hydrogen+Tritium, HyperNoblium+AntiNoblium, etc.) with escalating meltdownFlags (BaseExplosion/MediumExplosion/DevastatingExplosion, RadiationPulse, EMP, spread tiers up to CriticalMeltdown); HFRConsoleWindow.xaml shows exactly the four control dials (Heating Conductor, Cooling Volume, Magnetic Constrictor, Current Damper), mol/s injection spinboxes, and Fusion Level/Energy/Reaction Activity/Instability readouts; the construction graph gates every part's deconstruction on `HFRIsActive`, confirming it can't be unbolted while hot; and the entity file's HFRCore has GravityWell (the 'tugs at nearby objects' effect) plus a RadiationSource. The recipe file also confirms the graft_shape downgrade: fuel/moderator requirements and byproducts reference Hydrogen, Helium, HyperNoblium, AntiNoblium, BZ, Pluoxium, Halon, Zauker, Healium, ProtoNitrate and Nitrium, none of which are vanilla SS14 gases, so 'entangled' with an exotic-gas-expansion dependency is well-founded even though the fork's own files stay self-contained in _Funkystation namespaces (no upstream edits found). However several specific numbers in the gameplay prose don't match what's in the cited files: the file defines exactly 7 fusionRecipe entries, not eight; the console entity's only power figure is a 350 W ApcPowerReceiver, nowhere near '100 kW'; and '1 core + 4 corners + 3 edge pieces' sums to eight tiles, not the claimed nine.
  - unsupported: run it badly and it eats 100 kW — the only power figure in the cited files is the console's ApcPowerReceiver powerLoad: 350 (350 W), not 100 kW for the reactor
  - unsupported: eight fuel recipes with different risk profiles — hfr.yml defines exactly 7 fusionRecipe entries (plasmaO2, h2O2, t2O2, h2T2, hypernobHydrogen, hypernobTrit, hypernobAntinob)
  - unsupported: bolt together a nine-tile fusion machine ... a glowing core in the middle, four corners, and three edge pieces — 1 core + 4 corners + 3 edges sums to eight tiles, not nine, and the entity file only defines three distinct edge-piece types (fuel input, moderator input, waste output) so a true 3x3 grid (which needs 4 edge cells) isn't shown

### Singularity, tesla and radiation

<a id="singularity-and-tesla-engines"></a>

Containment-field engines (singularity and tesla) with emitters, a particle accelerator and grid radiation propagation.

**goobstation, serbia-strong**

*activity · needs upstream edits · medium confidence · 1 forks carry it*

Neither fork rebuilds the engine; both add small behavioural tweaks around it. On Goob, certain marked objects stop being flung away or destroyed when they touch a containment field, and certain marked things can sit inside a loose singularity without being eaten, so engineers can build setups that survive contact instead of everything near the field being scattered. Goob also gives radiation collectors "empty / low / full" output signals, so an engineer can wire collectors into an automated control setup that reacts when a tank runs dry or tops out. On SS220, a damaged RTG is a dying power source: its radiation output and the power it feeds the grid both bleed steadily down to nothing over about twenty minutes, so anything built around one is a temporary fix rather than a permanent generator.

- **Take** — Cheap, self-contained quality-of-life around an engine crew already interact with: field/singularity exemption tags stop legitimate builds getting shredded, and collector output signals let engineers automate the rad-collector loop instead of babysitting gauges.
- **Skip** — It is a handful of tweaks rather than a feature: the Goob half only works if you also patch upstream containment-field and event-horizon code to raise the cancellable events, the collector signals pull in Goob's factory automation layer, and none of the fetched files include the prototypes that actually attach any of these components, so you would be building the content side yourself.
- **Touches** — engineering, cargo, science
- **Needs** — [factory-automation](#factory-automation), [power-grid-and-device-networking](#power-grid-and-device-networking)
- **Verified** — supported. I fetched Content.Server/Singularity/EntitySystems/ContainmentFieldSystem.cs from both Goob-Station and space-wizards/space-station-14 and diffed them: upstream has no ContainmentFieldThrowEvent at all, while Goob's copy adds it inline with a '// Goobstation' comment marker and removes the mass check. That is direct, confirmed evidence the fork's own tree edits an upstream-namespaced file (Content.Server, not Content.Goobstation.*) in place, which both means the seed's path-only 'drop-in' guess was wrong (fork-patches-upstream) and that grafting elsewhere needs the same upstream edit (integration-would-require-upstream-edits) — hence 'both'. The claim's overall needs-upstream-edits label is therefore confirmed, but it overstates scope by also naming event-horizon code as needing a patch when that mechanism is unmodified vanilla.
  - unsupported: "the Goob half only works if you also patch upstream containment-field and event-horizon code to raise the cancellable events" — false for the event-horizon half. I diffed Content.Server/Singularity/Events/EventHorizonAttemptConsumeEntityEvent.cs and Content.Server/Singularity/EntitySystems/EventHorizonSystem.cs against upstream space-wizards/space-station-14 and they are byte-identical to vanilla: the cancellable AttemptConsumeEntity event already exists upstream with no Goob edits. EventHorizonIgnoreComponent/System is a genuine drop-in against that file. Only the containment-field half (ContainmentFieldSystem.cs, which upstream lacks ContainmentFieldThrowEvent entirely and Goob's copy adds it with an explicit '// Goobstation' marker) actually needs the upstream patch.

### Fission reactor

<a id="fission-reactor"></a>

A buildable multi-part nuclear reactor with fuel centrifuge, coolant loop, control computers and a steam or gas turbine as an alternative main power source.

**far-horizons**

*loop-change · needs upstream edits · high confidence · 4 forks carry it*

Engineers get a nuclear reactor as an alternative to the station's usual engine: a big vessel whose interior is a grid you physically fill in, slotting fuel rods, control rods, heat exchangers and gas channel pieces into a 5x5 or 7x7 layout, then piping cool gas in one side and running the hot gas out into a gas turbine that spins up and feeds the power grid. The control computer lets you flip between temperature, neutron and fuel views of the grid and raise or lower the control rods, and it will yell at you as the core climbs past dangerous into critical, with the reactor visibly smoking, catching fire, then triggering a station-wide meltdown announcement telling everyone to evacuate; a melted reactor fuses to the hull and cannot be unbolted. The turbine is its own maintenance job, with blades and stators that accumulate stress and damage, overspeed and stall warnings, welder repairs, and a failure mode where it tears itself apart and fires blade shrapnel across the room. Spent fuel goes into a centrifuge that reprocesses it into plutonium, and there are salvage-flavoured variants plus procedurally generated reactor complexes for crews to find derelict.

- **Take** — It is a genuinely deep, hands-on engine with a build-your-own-core puzzle, a real maintenance loop on the turbine, and a spectacular failure mode, all sitting in its own fork-namespaced folder rather than woven through upstream power code.
- **Skip** — The centrifuge (and likely more of the reactor) is a port from Goonstation carrying a CC-BY-NC-SA-3.0 header, which is non-commercial and does not sit cleanly alongside an AGPL fork licence, and beyond that it needs new sprites, new ores/materials (bohrum, cerenkite), guidebook pages, damage modifier sets and a map that actually has room for a reactor hall before any player sees it.
- **Touches** — engineering, atmospherics, cargo, salvage
- **Verified** — supported. Every specific gameplay beat checked out against the actual files: 5x5/7x7 grid prefabs with fuel rods/control rods/heat exchangers/gas channels (nuclear_reactor_prefabs.yml), temperature/neutron/fuel view toggle and control-rod raise/lower (nuclear-reactor.ftl, DeviceLinkSink InsertControlRods/RetractControlRods), dangerous->critical->smoke->fire->station-wide meltdown announcement telling people to evacuate (nuclear-reactor.ftl messages), melted reactor fused to the hull ("You cannot unanchor... it's melted into the hull!"), turbine blade/stator stress+damage+overspeed/stall+welder repair+explode-into-shrapnel (gas-turbine.ftl + GasTurbineBladeShrapnel projectile entity), spent fuel -> centrifuge -> plutonium (NuclearCentrifugeComponent.cs), salvage variants (NuclearReactorNormalSalvage etc.), and procedurally generated derelict reactor complexes (dungeon_presets.yml room packs ReactorBox/Long/Star/Double + Maps/_FarHorizons/Dungeon/Reactor). Nothing in the gameplay paragraph goes beyond what the files show. On graft shape: I cloned the repo and confirmed the license concern is real and verbatim ("Ported and modified from goonstation... CC-BY-NC-SA-3.0" in NuclearCentrifugeComponent.cs), so that part of skip_because is solid. I also confirmed every file for this feature (materials, sprites, guidebook pages, damage modifier sets, and even the fork's own parallel station map copies) lives under _FarHorizons namespaces only, i.e. Far Horizons itself never edits an upstream file in place - it forks its own full copies of station maps (Stations/Cog.yml, Manor.yml, meta.yml, etc.) rather than patching the vanilla ones. So the fork's own copy is self-contained (not fork-patches-upstream); the "needs-upstream-edits" label is earned because using this as an actual station engine (not just a derelict find) means a target fork must edit its OWN station maps to carve out a reactor hall, exactly the kind of upstream-adjacent map surgery Far Horizons already had to do for itself. One caveat worth flagging even though it doesn't rise to a gameplay-text overclaim: skip_because lists "new sprites, new ores/materials, guidebook pages, damage modifier sets" as outstanding costs, but I found all of these already fully built inside the fork's namespace (complete animated turbine/reactor .rsi sprite sheets, Bohrum/Cerenkite/Plutonium material defs, 5 guidebook XML pages, a StructuralReactorCasing damage set) - a graft would port these wholesale rather than create them from scratch. The map-room requirement is the one skip_because item that's genuinely still open.

### Factory automation

<a id="factory-automation"></a>

Automated production lines built from robotic arms, constructors, conveyors and label or stack filters that route and process items without a player.

**goobstation**

*activity · needs upstream edits · medium confidence · 3 forks carry it*

You can build a production line that keeps working while you walk away. Robotic arms sit next to machines and pick items up, feed them in, and pass the output along, and you slot a filter card into each arm to decide what it is allowed to grab: match a label, match part of an item's name, only take stacks above a certain size (and split off chunks of a set size), only take anchored or unanchored objects, only take mobs that are alive, dead, in crit, or handcuffed, or combine several filters with an AND/OR gate. A constructor machine can be told which recipe to start building, and further arms holding tools finish the multi-step assembly. On the chemistry side, plumbing pumps act as robotic arms for liquids, shifting reagents from one machine's tank into the next, with pressure filters gating flow to a chosen kPa band. Examining any arm or filter tells you what it is holding and what it is set to, and everything wires together with the normal signal-linker so you can gate a line on a button or sensor.

- **Take** — It turns "make 200 of these by hand" into a build-once machine, giving engineering and cargo a genuinely new mid-round project that runs unattended and gives quiet rounds something to do.
- **Skip** — It is a large surface (60+ code files across client, server and shared, six filter types each with its own UI window) and only pays off if enough upstream machines are tagged as automatable, which means touching existing machine prototypes and keeping that list current through every upstream sync; a half-ported version where only two machines accept arms is worse than not having it.
- **Touches** — engineering, cargo, science, medical, service
- **Verified** — supported. Cited files confirm the mechanics as described: filters.ftl shows label/name(Contain/Start/End/Match)/stack(min size + chunk size)/anchor/mob(Alive/Dead/Critical)/cuff filters plus a combined AND/OR gate filter; robotic-arm.ftl and PlumbingPumpComponent.cs confirm arm/plumbing-pump examine text and the "robotic arm for reagents" plumbing analogy with pressure-filter kPa bands; ConstructorComponent's doc comment ("Machine that starts constructions. Multi-step objects will need interactors to complete their steps") matches the constructor+tool-arm assembly claim; InteractorComponent's SinkPortPrototype field confirms normal signal-linker wiring. I went further than the cited evidence and pulled Resources/Prototypes/Entities/Structures/Machines/lathe.yml, microwave.yml, reagent_grinder.yml, chem_master.yml, fax_machine.yml and flatpacker.yml directly from the repo (not in the cited list) — these are upstream-namespace paths (no _Goobstation prefix) that the fork edits in place, adding `BaseAutomatedMachine` to the parent chain and an `AutomationSlots` component block, each tagged `# Goobstation`. That is direct proof the fork's own tree already patches upstream files (fork-patches-upstream), and it also validates the skip_because point that extending the feature means touching more upstream machine prototypes on every sync (integration-would-require-upstream-edits for anyone wiring this into a different codebase). Both readings hold simultaneously here.

### Warp drive

<a id="warp-drive"></a>

Lets the whole station or ship warp between locations, including an interruption state that throws entities out of normal space.

**ephemeral-space**

*structural · entangled · high confidence · 0 forks carry it*

A big Gravitational Warp Drive sits in a public room on the station, apparently haunted by a talkative entity that spends the whole round making unsettling announcements about how everyone is doing. It charges on its own for roughly 45-50 minutes, and getting it fully charged and fired is how the crew wins the round. Anyone can walk into the drive itself, which dumps them into a weird pocket dimension and then spits them back out somewhere random on the station a bit dazed. The drive gets "clogged" at random, and traitors can clog it deliberately by throwing junk in; charging halts until someone climbs inside and picks the stuck items out, which is worth doing anyway since the debris is sometimes valuable loot. Once it hits full charge, the crew has two minutes to run to three scattered security override terminals (the same terminals traitors use for nuke codes) and activate all three, then activate the console in the drive room to start a countdown to a guaranteed win.

- **Take** — It gives the crew an actual win condition with a visible timer, a sabotage surface antags can attack all round, and a frantic three-terminal endgame scramble, all wrapped in a genuinely memorable talking-machine character.
- **Skip** — It is the spine of Ephemeral Space's round structure, not a bolt-on: the system pulls in that fork's objective framework, its crypto-nuke terminal rework, its announcement, cinematic and timer systems, a bespoke pocket-dimension map, and station mapping for the drive room and three terminals, so grafting it means importing most of a round design and then remapping every station you run.
- **Touches** — all-players, command, engineering, science, antagonist, security
- **Needs** — [antag-objectives-and-uplink-rework](#antag-objectives-and-uplink-rework), [alternate-round-types](#alternate-round-types), [nuclear-operatives](#nuclear-operatives), [custom-station-maps](#custom-station-maps)
- **Verified** — supported. Read the guidebook (WarpDrive.xml), the game-rule yml, the announcement/screen/popup locale files, and ESWarpDriveSystem.cs directly. Every specific gameplay beat in the claim (public-access drive, ~45-50 min charge, pocket-dimension teleport with a dazing debuff, random/sabotage-able clogs whose cleared debris is loot, the fully-charged 2-minute three-terminal scramble shared with nuke codes, then a console activation starting a guaranteed-win countdown) is verbatim or near-verbatim in the guidebook text and locale strings. On graft shape: ESWarpDriveSystem.cs imports and actively calls into Content.Server._ES.Objectives (ESObjectiveSystem), Content.Server._ES.Announcements (ESAnnouncementSystem), Content.Shared._ES.Cinematic (ESCinematicSystem/PlayCinematicEvent), Content.Shared._ES.Core.Timer, and Content.Shared._ES.Nuke.Components (ESCryptoNukeSecurityOverridenEvent, and the guidebook explicitly says the override terminals are the same ESBaseComputerTerminalCryptoNuke entities used by nuclear-operatives), plus a bespoke Resources/Maps/_ES/singularity_world.yml pocket-dimension map confirmed via directory listing. That is real, load-bearing cross-feature coupling within the fork's own _ES tree, not just a stray import - it contradicts the 'drop-in' seed and supports the claim's downgrade to 'entangled' and its depends_on list (nuclear-operatives and antag-objectives-and-uplink-rework are directly confirmed in code; custom-station-maps is supported by the bespoke map; alternate-round-types is plausible via GameRuleSystem/RoundEndSystem usage but less directly nailed down).

### Atmospherics simulation

<a id="atmospherics-simulation"></a>

Tile-based gas simulation with mixtures, reactions, pipe networks, vents, scrubbers, air alarms, canisters and space wind.

**backmen, deltav, frontier, funky, serbia-strong, sunrise**

*activity · needs upstream edits · medium confidence · 6 forks carry it*

Six forks pile extra things to do on top of the standard gas game. Frontier turns atmospherics into a paying job outside the station: you fly an atmos ship out to an asteroid, sweep it with a handheld deposit scanner that beeps as you close in, dig out a frozen whisp of oxygen, plasma, helium or nitrogen, bolt a mining drill onto it, run pipes to the rock's edge and dock your shuttle through a portable airlock-for-gas so the drill fills your onboard tanks, then filter the mix and sell it by canister or by the tankful at a sale point that pays more the purer your gas is. Funky adds bigger toys for the atmos tech at home: a hypertorus fusion reactor built from a core, console and side parts, a crystallizer that solidifies gases, and a bluespace sender that pipes gas across the map to linked vendors. The rest are smaller touches players feel rather than build: a smart gas mask with its own action button and readout, gas tanks that top themselves back up, a redesigned atmospheric alerts console, and visible motes blowing past when air rushes into space.

- **Take** — Frontier's offshore gas mining is the rare thing that gives atmospherics a reason to leave its room: a full scan-drill-dock-filter-sell loop with its own guidebook page, tools and payout curve, aimed squarely at the department that usually has nothing to do after setup.
- **Skip** — Almost none of it is portable as-is: Frontier's loop only makes sense on a fork where players own and fly dockable ships and can sell cargo, Funky's reactor and crystallizer are whole new machines with construction graphs and C# systems behind them, and Sunrise's and SS220's pieces are partial-class patches onto the upstream tile atmosphere and barotrauma code, so you would be maintaining edits inside the engine's hottest loop across every upstream sync.
- **Touches** — engineering, atmospherics, cargo, salvage, all-players
- **Needs** — [exotic-gas-expansion](#exotic-gas-expansion), [shipyard-player-ships](#shipyard-player-ships)
- **Verified** — partly supported. The core of the claim checks out hard: Frontier's OffshoreGasMining.xml guidebook and its gas-deposit/gas-sale locale files confirm the full scan-drill-dock-filter-sell loop with purity-based payout exactly as described; Funky's hfr.yml and crystallizer.yml confirm the hypertorus reactor (core/console/side-part) and crystallizer; bluespace_gas.yml confirms the cross-map bluespace sender to linked vendors; SS220's smart_gas_mask.yml confirms an Action-driven gas mask; Backmen's spacewind.yml confirms the despawning "space wind motes" visual effect. But two of the twelve cited files do not back their claims: _Funkystation/.../Specific/Atmospherics/vox.yml 404s (the whole Structures/Specific directory doesn't exist in funky-station), so "gas tanks that top themselves back up" has no supporting evidence at all; and _DV/engineering/warnings.ftl contains only a single AME antimatter-fuel-warning string, nothing about an atmospheric alerts console, so "redesigned atmospheric alerts console" is also unsupported by its cited file. On graft_shape, I independently confirmed needs-upstream-edits is the right call, and found instances of both readings: Sunrise's Content.Server/Atmos/TileAtmosphere.cs is edited in place (partial class marked "// Sunrise-edit" with inline "Sunrise-Start/End" blocks) inside the actual upstream file, i.e. fork-patches-upstream is real for at least this fork; meanwhile Frontier/Funky/Backmen/SS220's cited prototypes all live in their own _NF/_Funkystation/_Backmen/SS220 namespaces with no upstream edits visible in what I fetched, matching integration-would-require-upstream-edits for those forks' pieces. Given the seed explicitly can't see in-place upstream edits, this is exactly the kind of unit where manual settlement was needed, and the verdict holds.

  - unsupported: a redesigned atmospheric alerts console

### Planet weather and fog

<a id="planet-weather-and-fog"></a>

Surface-level environmental simulation for planetary maps: weather effects, fog that hides the map before deployment and temperature effects outdoors.

**rmc14**

*loop-change · entangled · medium confidence · 0 forks carry it*

On RMC-14's planet maps the sky is doing something: dust storms and blowing sand on the red desert, snow, blizzards and driving rain on the frozen and urban maps, each with its own looping storm audio, so an outdoor firefight looks and sounds different from an indoor one. At round start the map also picks one of several pre-placed blocker groups and clears it, so which routes out of the landing zone are open changes between rounds while the rest stay walled off. The bulk of what actually ships here, though, is a fire rework: burning tiles left behind by flamethrowers that linger for the better part of a minute, characters catching fire and dropping and rolling to put themselves out, a teammate patting the flames off you, molotovs crafted from bottles, and rounds that ignite what they hit, with per-creature immunities and armour penalties layered on top.

- **Touches** — all-players, security, antagonist, engineering
- **Needs** — [custom-station-maps](#custom-station-maps), [xenomorph-hive](#xenomorph-hive), [shared-utility-libraries](#shared-utility-libraries)
- **Verified** — partly supported. Fetched all six cited files directly. weather.yml confirms looping storm audio + per-biome overlay sprites (dust/sand/snow/blizzard/rain) exactly as described. TileFireComponent's Duration=55s matches "the better part of a minute". Browsing Content.Shared/_RMC14/Atmos turned up ~29 more fire-specific files (molotov crafting, stop-drop-roll, fire-patting, per-creature immunity/bypass components, armor-debuff modifiers, projectile ignition) that substantiate the fire-rework description almost line for line, and RMCFlammableSystem.cs derives from upstream FlammableSystem/FlammableComponent while SharedRMCFlammableSystem.cs (1179 lines) imports Content.Shared._RMC14.Xenonids.Plasma, .Map, .Armor, .Vehicle, .Explosion, .Weapons.Melee, and .Emote — confirming, and actually understating, the claimed entanglement with RMC14's other own systems (xeno plasma, map, and beyond). Nothing in the file ties this to 'landing zone' routes specifically; that's a plausible RMC14-lore inference, not something the cited code confirms.

**gaby-station-now-dumont-station, starlight, the-den**

*activity · needs upstream edits · medium confidence · 0 forks carry it*

Three small planetside atmosphere additions. Gaby's is a "Faithless" weather set: light, medium and heavy layers of crawling static that wash over the screen outdoors, each with its own looping ambient track, plus a heavier "hell" variant with an alternate soundscape, so being outside on that map gets progressively noisier and harder to see through. Starlight adds a spawner you drop on a map that kicks off weather after a delay and can end it after a set time, and makes weather actually bite: anyone standing under open sky periodically takes whatever effect the storm carries (damage, cold, chemical exposure) scaled by how strong it is, with a matching screen tint. The Den adds a planetary day/night cycle where outdoor light colour walks through a palette across an in-game day at roughly a minute every four seconds, so a shift visibly runs from noon into dusk and night.

- **Take** — Cheap way to make outdoor and planet play feel like a place: storms that actually hurt exposed players, dread ambience, and lighting that visibly moves through a day.
- **Skip** — None of the three pieces is a whole feature on its own, and they only pay off if you already run planet or surface maps worth standing outside on; the audio/sprite half is bespoke art you would have to license or redraw.
- **Touches** — all-players, cargo, science
- **Verified** — supported. Decisive evidence: Starlight's Content.Server/_Starlight/Weather/WeatherSystem.Effect.cs is a `namespace Content.Server.Weather` partial-class extension, and the vanilla Content.Server/Weather/WeatherSystem.cs (39 lines, no fork prefix) contains literal `InitEffects();` / `UpdateEffects(frameTime);` calls that only exist because of this fork's code — the fork's own copy has edited an upstream-namespaced file in place, confirming fork-patches-upstream for that piece. Separately, the Gaby weather YAML and The Den's TimeCycle system (Content.Shared/TimeCycle + Content.Server/TimeCycle, no fork-namespace prefix but self-contained, hooking only via existing MapLightComponent) are clean new files that would still need YAML/prototype wiring to activate on a target codebase's maps, i.e. integration-would-require-upstream-edits for those pieces. The combined three-fork unit legitimately needs both readings.
  - unsupported: "(damage, cold, chemical exposure)" — the only two configured WeatherEntityEffect examples found (WeatherRadStorm, WeatherSolarFlare in Resources/Prototypes/_Starlight/Entities/StatusEffects/weather.yml) use HealthChange (radiation/heat damage) and AdjustTemperature; no chemical/reagent-exposure weather prototype was found, so that third example is inferred from the generic EntityEffect[] capability rather than observed in a shipped prototype.
  - unsupported: "touches": ["cargo", "science"] — nothing in the cited evidence (weather prototypes, marker/effect components, day-night system) ties this feature to cargo or science departments; this looks like an uncorroborated catalog tag rather than something derived from the files.

### Spreading fire

<a id="spreading-fire-system"></a>

Fire that lives on the floor as its own layer, spreading from tile to tile or igniting from flammable spilled reagents with origin tracking and tunable behaviour.

**ephemeral-space**

*loop-change · needs upstream edits · high confidence · 2 forks carry it*

Fire becomes a thing that sits on the floor and creeps: a burning tile crackles with its own flame sprite and sound, slows anyone who walks through it, scorches the floor with burn marks, and once a second tries to jump to a neighbouring tile, preferring tiles that are already hot and skipping ones with no oxygen or nothing flammable to catch. Flames come in four visible intensities and burn themselves down as they spread, eventually smouldering to a weaker flame or dying out on their own, so a blaze that gets going grows into a wandering front the crew has to cut off rather than a single fire they stand next to and extinguish. Anything that triggers, from a thrown incendiary to a rigged device, can drop a fire of a chosen intensity, and every fire remembers who started it, so an arsonist's whole spreading blaze is traceable back to them.

- **Take** — It turns fire from a per-entity status effect into a spatial hazard that moves through the station, giving atmos and engineering an actual firefighting job and giving arsonist play a real tool.
- **Skip** — It is not the self-contained fork-namespaced drop-in it looks like: the prototype leans on flammable fields (firestack visual divisor, minimum/maximum firestacks, delete-on-extinguish, basic fire spread) and a per-tile Flammability value that upstream does not have, so grafting it means patching upstream flammable and tile-definition code and then re-patching them on every sync.
- **Touches** — engineering, atmospherics, security, antagonist, all-players
- **Verified** — supported. Every gameplay beat checks out in the actual code: the ESTileFire prototype has four staged sprites/sounds (red_1..4, fire1..4.ogg), SpeedModifierContacts 0.8/0.8 for the floor-slow, TryAddBurntDecalsToTile for scorch marks, edge_spreaders.yml sets updatesPerSecond:1 for spread cadence, OnSpreadNeighbors weights neighbor tiles up for high temperature and zeroes tiles with tileDef.Flammability<=0 or low oxygen, fires lose firestacks on each spread (AdjustFireStacks negative) and the Update() loop either deletes or downgrades to a weaker stage once SmolderTime passes, ESTileFireOnTriggerComponent lets any BaseXOnTriggerComponent consumer (grenades, rigged devices) spawn a chosen Stage, and Origin/ESTileFireOriginComponent propagate through every child fire spawned by a spread, so a whole blaze traces to one originating entity. I then went beyond the cited evidence to settle the graft_shape question, diffing the fork's own Content.Shared/Atmos/Components/FlammableComponent.cs and Content.Shared/Maps/ContentTileDefinition.cs against space-wizards/space-station-14 master. Both files are NOT under the _ES/ namespace and both carry literal '// ES START ... // ES END' blocks in the fork's own tree: FlammableComponent.cs adds FirestackVisualDivisor, DeleteOnExtinguish, BasicFireSpread (and several atmos-energy fields the tile-fire system doesn't even use); ContentTileDefinition.cs adds the Flammability field the spread-scoring code reads. That is direct proof the fork edits upstream-named files in place, not just files that would need editing to integrate elsewhere - the needs-upstream-edits downgrade from the drop-in seed is correct, and correct in the stronger 'fork-patches-upstream' sense. One inaccuracy in the claim's own reasoning: it lists 'minimum/maximum firestacks' as fields 'upstream does not have', but upstream FlammableComponent.cs already defines MinimumFireStacks and MaximumFireStacks (and FireSpread) - only FirestackVisualDivisor, DeleteOnExtinguish and BasicFireSpread are actually new. This doesn't change the verdict (real new fields still force upstream edits) but the claim overstates which specific fields are novel.

**forky**

*loop-change · needs upstream edits · high confidence · 2 forks carry it*

Spilled flammable liquid stops being scenery. Get a puddle of welding fuel, booze or other volatile chemistry hot enough (a welder, a hotspot, hot air on the tile) and it catches: the tile lights up with a roaring looping fire sound and a coloured flame that runs orange for weak mixes up through yellow to white-hot for the really volatile stuff, and the puddle visibly burns itself down. While it burns it heats the air on that tile, eats oxygen and belches CO2 and steam, leaves scorch marks on the floor, and reaches into the four neighbouring tiles: any puddle next door catches too, so a spill trail (and, if the server allows it, wet footprints) carries fire across a room, though walls and closed airlocks stop it. Anyone standing in the flames takes burn and structural damage each second, cut down by fire-protective gear, and a thin dribble burns out fast and weak while a big pool burns long and hot.

- **Take** — It gives every flammable spill real physical consequence, chaining chemistry, welding, atmos and arson-flavoured sabotage into one hazard that firefighters actually have to chase across a room, and every knob (damage, volume scaling, footprint flammability, gear protection) is a server CVar rather than a code change.
- **Skip** — It is a per-second per-tile fire sim doing entity lookups, decal writes, atmos mutation and damage on every burning puddle, and it is bolted to fork-only plumbing (a Funky `TileExposedEvent` carrying a spark source, a fork `TileFireEvent`, and the fork's footprint component) plus Starfall-style particle prototypes, so grafting it means importing or re-pointing that atmos wiring and accepting a spill-chain performance risk.
- **Touches** — engineering, atmospherics, medical, chemistry, security, antagonist, all-players
- **Needs** — [atmospherics-simulation](#atmospherics-simulation), [visual-feedback-effects](#visual-feedback-effects)
- **Verified** — partly supported. All five cited files fetched cleanly and back almost the entire gameplay description: TileExposedEvent-driven ignition with a per-flammability ignition temperature, colour scaling orange→white via GetFireColor, a looping bigfire.ogg sound, per-second burn that heats the tile, consumes O2, produces CO2/water vapor, drops burnt1-4 decals, spreads to the 4 cardinal neighbour tiles, damages standing entities (Heat+Structural) each second reduced by FireProtectionComponent, volume-scaled burn rate (small puddles burn fast/weak via SmallPuddleBurnThreshold/Percent, big ones slow via VolumeScalingReference/Curve), and every tunable (damage, footprint flammability, protection effectiveness, volume curve) is indeed a server-only CVar in ReagentFireCVars.cs. However, I re-read the neighbour-spread loop closely: the `isBlocked` (AirtightComponent) check only gates the atmos heat-radiation branch — the `foreach (var adjPuddle in GetPuddlesOnTile(...)) Ignite(adjPuddle, ...)` call right below runs unconditionally with no isBlocked check, so a puddle on the far side of a closed airlock/wall tile still ignites directly. The claim's 'walls and closed airlocks stop it' is not supported by the code as written. Separately and more importantly for graft_shape: I traced who raises the fork's TileExposedEvent and found it is not raised from any _Funkystation file — it's injected into the vanilla Content.Server/Atmos/EntitySystems/AtmosphereSystem.Hotspot.cs (inside HotspotExpose, wrapped in literal '// Funky start'/'// Funky end' comments), and the fork's TileFireEvent is likewise subscribed to inside the vanilla Content.Server/Atmos/EntitySystems/FlammableSystem.cs (SubscribeLocalEvent<FlammableComponent, TileFireEvent>). Both are genuine upstream-namespaced files edited in place, not fork files sitting in upstream directories by coincidence — this directly falsifies the 'drop-in' path-data seed and confirms the assessor's needs-upstream-edits call, specifically as fork-patches-upstream rather than merely a hypothetical integration cost.
  - unsupported: though walls and closed airlocks stop it

## Cargo

### Vending machines and container fills

<a id="vending-and-loot-catalogs"></a>

Fork-specific vending machine rosters with their own inventories and ad barks, plus the crate, locker, box and maintenance loot tables that stock the station.

**ephemeral-space**

*activity · entangled · medium confidence · 11 forks carry it*

Adds a set of station-flavour vending machines with their own product lists and chatty ad barks, including a pride-clothing "Gender Bash" dispenser, a scrap-dealer machine hawking military and engineering surplus scavenged from derelicts, a plain water cooler, and a lumber-and-welding-fuel machine that warns you not to light fires indoors. Their stock is rolled from loot tables at round start rather than being a fixed shelf, so two rounds of the same machine can offer different goods. It also rewrites what you find when you crack open lockers, dressers, wardrobes, backpacks, briefcases and maintenance crates: theatre wardrobes hand out whole themed costumes (jester, chicken suit, cowboy in one of three colours, shrine maiden, Santa), and there are hidden ceiling caches that spawn a matched antagonist kit, for example a silenced pistol with spare magazine, sleepy pens and smoke grenades, or a chameleon backpack with an emag and C4.

- **Take** — Randomised, table-driven vending stock plus themed costume and cache fills is a cheap way to make looting and maintenance scavenging feel different every round, and the machinery for it is a single small fork-namespaced component and system.
- **Skip** — The content is only as good as the entity ids it points at: the traitor caches pull in the fork's own guns, magazines, emag and chameleon backpack and its assassin/infiltrator/marauder/subverter archetypes, so those tables need rewriting against your own item set, and the vending machines are inert until someone places them on your maps.
- **Touches** — cargo, service, salvage, antagonist, all-players
- **Needs** — [firearms-content-expansion](#firearms-content-expansion), [traitor-uplink](#traitor-uplink)
- **Verified** — partly supported; assessed as drop-in, corrected by the verifier. All files I fetched are namespace-contained under _ES (and DatasetVocalizer at Content.Server/Vocalization exists identically in wizden upstream, so no fork patch), but the vendor prototypes in vending.yml embed ESAmbientMusicMarker* components from the fork's ambient-music unit and a fork guidebook ref, the cache tables reference ES weapons/emag/uplink items, and the headline ceiling-cache gameplay only exists via the fork's SecretIdentity system — two undisclosed cross-unit dependencies beyond the two listed in depends_on.
  - unsupported: "a plain water cooler" — the machine is a 'suspicious water vendor' ('It looks normal...?') whose fill rolls half its stock from SuspiciousWaterTable; it is a trap/joke vendor, not a plain water dispenser
  - unsupported: "so two rounds of the same machine can offer different goods" — true for Salvaged Sam's, the water vendor, and Woodgrain (prob/rolls selectors), but the Gender Bash vendor's inventory is a fixed all-selector with fixed amounts and is identical every round
  - unsupported: "there are hidden ceiling caches that spawn a matched antagonist kit" — this unit's caches.yml only defines ordinary CrateGenericSteel prototypes and loot tables (the 'hidden in the ceiling' description is commented out); the ceiling-hiding, reveal alert, and mind-matched spawning are implemented in Content.Shared/_ES/SecretIdentity/Traitor/ (ESCeilingCacheComponent, ESSecretIdentityCacheSpawnerComponent), a separate system depending on _ES/Core/Timer, _ES/SpawnRegion and an Alert prototype, none of which is in this unit or its depends_on list; the caches also include crew archetypes (mercenary, insider, arms dealer, hitman), not only antagonist kits
  - unsupported: "the machinery for it is a single small fork-namespaced component and system" — true only for vendor fills; locker/crate/cache fills use upstream EntityTableContainerFill, and the cache-delivery machinery is a separate multi-file SecretIdentity system

**impstation**

*activity · entangled · high confidence · 11 forks carry it*

Impstation stocks the station with its own branded vending machines that chatter their own ad barks: a sports-drink cooler pushing "healthy bodies, healthy bottom line", a Discount Dan's shrimp-snack machine that warns you the snacks "cannot and will not smile back", a juice machine that nags you about booze, a salvage wardrobe selling mining gear with jokes about fresh-looking corpses, and Deadly Dan's, which sells a cheap disposable pistol and hidden ammo behind lines like "Safety feature? The point is to be Deadly!" Each machine also has a wire-hacked contraband row (a sniper rifle, a clown mask, a cigarette pack) so breaking one open is worth doing. Alongside that, the crates cargo can order and the lockers, closets and boxes scattered around the map are refilled from fork tables, so you order a princess dress-up crate, a theremin, a drum kit or a box of 500 cigarettes, and the wall closets you pry open hold the fork's own uniform and clothing sets rather than the stock ones.

- **Take** — It is the cheapest possible way to make a station feel like your fork: pure YAML lists of items, ad lines and prices, no C# at all, and you can adopt one vendor or one crate at a time.
- **Skip** — Almost every entry points at Impstation's own items (shrimp snacks, Asterade sodas, the Valu pistol, fork instruments and plushies), so a naive copy yields a wall of missing-prototype errors unless you first port the content those lists sell; and several fill files reuse upstream prototype ids like ClosetWallAtmosphericsFilled, which collides with the upstream definitions rather than sitting quietly beside them.
- **Touches** — cargo, salvage, service, security, all-players
- **Needs** — [food-and-drink-expansion](#food-and-drink-expansion), [clothing-and-wardrobe-pack](#clothing-and-wardrobe-pack), [firearms-content-expansion](#firearms-content-expansion), [object-and-tool-art](#object-and-tool-art)
- **Verified** — partly supported; assessed as needs upstream edits, corrected by the verifier. Every cited evidence file lives under _Impstation-namespaced Locale/Prototype directories, and even the actual map placements I traced (ClosetWallOrangeFilled, VendingMachineSalvDrobe) sit in Impstation's own separate Resources/Maps/_Impstation/oasis.yml, not in an edited copy of an upstream map — I checked upstream's shared box.yml and bagel.yml directly and found zero references to any of this unit's fork-specific prototype ids. That contradicts the claim's specific 'collides with upstream ClosetWallAtmosphericsFilled' reasoning (no such id exists upstream; I checked all 14 upstream Locker fill files). The real, well-confirmed blocker is that these YAML tables reference dozens of Impstation-exclusive item ids (FoodSnackDanShrimpsnax*, DrinkOrangeAsteradeBottleFull, WeaponPistolValu, ClothingUniformPinkPrincessDress, ThereminInstrument, etc.) that only resolve if you also bring in the fork's other named content packages — a sibling-content dependency (entangled), not literal upstream-file patching.
  - unsupported: "the wall closets you pry open hold the fork's own uniform and clothing sets rather than the stock ones" — the actual wardrobe_job.yml fill (ClothingUniformJumpsuitAtmos, ClothingBackpackEngineering, ClothingShoesColorWhite for the atmos closet; ClothingUniformJumpsuitPrisoner, ClothingShoesColorBlack, ClothingMaskMuzzle for the orange closet) are stock/vanilla SS14 clothing ids, not Impstation-branded sets; upstream's own equivalent closet (ClosetWallWardrobeAtmosphericsFilled) fills with nearly the same items.
  - unsupported: skip_because's specific claim "several fill files reuse upstream prototype ids like ClosetWallAtmosphericsFilled, which collides with the upstream definitions" — checked every file in upstream space-wizards/space-station-14's Resources/Prototypes/Catalog/Fills/Lockers/ directory directly; no prototype with id ClosetWallAtmosphericsFilled exists anywhere upstream (upstream's actual equivalent id is the differently-named ClosetWallWardrobeAtmosphericsFilled). The cited collision is not supported.
  - unsupported: "Each machine also has a wire-hacked contraband row (a sniper rifle, a clown mask, a cigarette pack)" reads as one shared three-item contraband set; in fact each machine's contrabandInventory has exactly one item, spread across three different machines (WeaponSniperMosin on deadlydan, ClothingMaskClownCargo on salvdrobe, CigPackShrimp on danshrimp).

**rmc14**

*loop-change · entangled · medium confidence · 11 forks carry it*

Instead of a machine that spits out one item per click, RMC-14's vendors open a shop window with named tabs (Ammo, Smokables, Radio Keys, Kits) where every item carries a price and you spend a personal budget that the machine remembers per person. Vendors only unlock for the right job or rank, some categories let you take exactly one thing and then close for you, some hand you a pre-filled box instead of a loose item, and squad specialist kits are limited server-wide so once two people have claimed a kit nobody else can. Buying certain kits also rewrites your visible role title, name prefix and map marker, so the crew can see what you picked. Points can trickle back over time on some machines, a machine with the right engineering know-how can be hacked open after a short delay to bypass its access lock, and anyone can top a machine back up by feeding it spare stock.

- **Take** — Turns "walk to vending machine, click item" into a real per-character equipment budget with scarcity, role gating and public role identity, which gives every department a meaningful loadout decision at round start instead of a free-for-all grab.
- **Skip** — The vendor gating is wired straight into RMC-14's rank, skill and squad systems (rank lists, an engineering skill level for hacking, squad mapping, global specialist-kit caps), so grafting it means either importing those systems or rewriting every gate, and then hand-authoring an entire priced catalogue per machine before a single one is usable.
- **Touches** — all-players, command, security, medical, cargo, service
- **Needs** — [squads-ranks-and-skills](#squads-ranks-and-skills), [loadout-system](#loadout-system)
- **Verified** — partly supported. Core mechanics check out against source: CMAutomatedVendorComponent has Jobs/Ranks lists, Hackable/HackSkill="RMCSkillEngineer"/HackSkillLevel=2/HackDelay, CanManualRestock, and points-per-person via CMVendorUserComponent.Points. CMVendorSection has named sections (confirmed live in portable_vendor.yml with tabs like "Smokables"/"Radio keys"/"Ammo"), TakeOne/TakeAll, and Box/BoxAmount/BoxSlots for pre-filled containers (HasBoxes). RMCVendorSpecialistComponent.GlobalSharedVends + SharedCMAutomatedVendorSystem.cs (lines ~610-650) confirm a server-wide shared cap that sums vends across every vendor instance and blocks once the total hits the section's SharedSpecLimit. But I grepped the entire _RMC14 prototype tree (2012 yml files) and found exactly one live SharedSpecLimit value in the whole repo: `specialist.yml:13: sharedSpecLimit: 1`, not 2 — so per the actual data the cap is "one person claims it and it's gone," not "once two people have claimed it." Role-title/prefix/icon/map-blip rewrite on purchase is real (GiveSquadRoleName/GivePrefix/GiveIcon/GiveMapBlip fields, all populated in Squad/specialist.yml with rmc-job-name-weapons-specialist-* strings). Recharge-over-time is real but used by exactly one job (Liaison) via RMCVendorUserRechargeComponent — "some machines" is defensible as-is. Manual restock (CanManualRestock) is used by several vendors (intel, pilot, requisitions, squad engineer/prep). Hackable is used on several PVE-faction vendors. On graft_shape: the claim already downgraded the path-data "drop-in" seed to "entangled," citing squads-ranks-and-skills + loadout-system. I confirm the ranks/skills half hard: RankPrototype and SkillDefinitionComponent (engineer skill for hacking) are DataFields directly on the vendor component, not optional. The loadout-system half is weaker than claimed: I found zero references to "loadout" anywhere in Content.Shared/_RMC14/Vendors/*.cs, and the two loadout evidence files cited (civilian.yml patches, backpacks.yml satchels) belong to the separate character-creation loadout/cost system with no code path connecting it to vendors that I could find. That doesn't change the bottom-line verdict — ranks+jobs+skills entanglement alone is sufficient to keep this "entangled," not drop-in — but the depends_on list overstates the loadout-system link specifically.
  - unsupported: squad specialist kits are limited server-wide so once two people have claimed a kit nobody else can

### Cargo bounties, contracts and markets

<a id="cargo-bounties-and-market"></a>

Extends cargo beyond ordering with player-posted bounty contracts, market consoles, trade crates with destination routing and delivery-based hauling work.

**rmc14**

*loop-change · entangled · high confidence · 3 forks carry it*

The supply tech works a counter rather than a console: crew queue up at a shutter and ask for gear by name, and the tech decides whether each request is reasonable before handing it over from a bank of specialist vendors. Bigger or rarer orders go through an ASRS terminal that spends a shared budget, and the goods physically arrive on a cargo elevator that has to be raised and lowered — standing in the open pit while it comes down is genuinely lethal. Every delivered crate comes with a printed invoice listing its contents; the tech tears it off, stamps it approved and returns it for a cash rebate, and empty crates are re-packed by hand and set on colour-coded launch pads so command (or the tech, for the emergency pad, using coordinates radioed up from the ground) can fire them down to a team fighting elsewhere.

- **Take** — It turns cargo from a menu-and-wait chore into an actual shift of work: a physical delivery elevator, hand-packed crates, stamped invoices for income, and a remote drop system that makes the supply role matter to people who are nowhere near the department.
- **Skip** — Almost none of it is portable as-is: the catalogue is wall-to-wall RMC-specific ammunition and attachment crates, the drop pads are keyed to that fork's squad system, and the elevator/pit and pad layout are built into their map, so you would be reimplementing the loop rather than copying it.
- **Touches** — cargo, command, engineering, all-players
- **Needs** — [squads-ranks-and-skills](#squads-ranks-and-skills), [firearms-content-expansion](#firearms-content-expansion)
- **Verified** — supported. Fetched RMCRequisitions.xml, requisitions_catalog.yml, RequisitionsSystem.Rewards.cs, and SupplyDropComputerComponent.cs directly. The guidebook text confirms, near verbatim, the counter/shutter workflow, tech judgment on requests, the four vendor bank, the ASRS terminal's shared budget, the Pit elevator (RequisitionsElevatorComponent has a ChasmCheckEvery field and the guide warns "you might not wake up" when lowered), printed/stamped invoices for a cash reward (PrintInvoice + SubmitInvoices in RequisitionsSystem.Rewards.cs), and the five colour-coded drop pads with CIC controlling four squad pads and the tech controlling the coordinate-fed Echo pad. The catalog file is 417 lines of RMC-specific ammo/attachment crates, and SupplyDropComputerComponent.cs has a hard `EntProtoId<SquadTeamComponent>? Squad` field, directly substantiating the claim's own downgrade from the seed's 'drop-in' guess to 'entangled' via a real dependency on the fork's squad system plus firearms-specific content.

**white-dream**

*activity · needs upstream edits · medium confidence · 3 forks carry it*

A glowing red target circle burns onto the floor with a long incoming-mortar whistle, and about ten seconds later something drops out of the sky onto that spot: a supply pod that cracks open with a small blast and spills its contents, or a rocket that just detonates. The pods come in a range of flavours and payloads, from a surplus cargo crate of random goods to Syndicate surplus bundles worth anywhere from 5 to 125 telecrystals, a Cybersun Juggernaut kit, or a live gondola that wanders off. Crew who see the marker get a few seconds to sprint toward the free loot or run away from it, and the landed pods stay behind as containers you can pry open, weld apart for steel, or even build yourself from three steel sheets.

- **Take** — It turns any loot delivery into a telegraphed, dodgeable event the whole room reacts to, and the whole thing is prototype-only YAML built on generic spawner/despawn components.
- **Skip** — Despite sitting under the cargo-market heading it posts no bounties and runs no market: it is a delivery-and-spectacle wrapper around payloads upstream already hands out, and it drags in the fork's own telegraph, falling-pod and rocket sprites plus a custom whistle sound before it looks like anything.
- **Touches** — cargo, antagonist, all-players, admin
- **Verified** — partly supported; assessed as drop-in, corrected by the verifier. The telegraph/pod/rocket flavor description checks out against the cited YAML (red target circle, 10s TimedSpawner + 12s TimedDespawn, mortar whistle sound, SmallExplosionInstant crack-open, MediumExplosionInstant for rockets, 5/10/15/20/25/50/125 TK syndicate SurplusBundle tiers, CybersunJuggernautBundle StorageFill, MobGondola). But the feature is not "prototype-only YAML built on generic spawner/despawn components": the actual implementation of the Syndicate surplus loot lives in Content.Server/Traitor/Uplink/SurplusBundle/SurplusBundleComponent.cs and SurplusBundleSystem.cs, brand-new C# files sitting inside the upstream Traitor/Uplink directory (not under _White), and that system calls Content.Server.Store.Systems.StoreSystem.GetAvailableListings against the vanilla uplink Store/currency prototypes (StorePresetUplink in Resources/Prototypes/Store/presets.yml) to pick which Telecrystal-priced items go in each bundle. None of this C# or the Store dependency was in evidence_cited. That is a real dependency the seed's drop-in path-scan missed (it only scanned _White-prefixed prototype paths), so this should be downgraded off drop-in.
  - unsupported: "the whole thing is prototype-only YAML built on generic spawner/despawn components" (take_because) — the Syndicate surplus-bundle payloads are generated by custom C# (SurplusBundleSystem.cs) that queries the upstream Store/Uplink catalog system at runtime, not by static YAML on generic components.
  - unsupported: "depends_on": [] — the syndicate bundle path genuinely depends on Content.Server.Store.Systems.StoreSystem and the vanilla uplink categories/currency (StorePresetUplink, Resources/Prototypes/Store/presets.yml), which is not listed as a dependency.

**starlight**

*loop-change · needs upstream edits · medium confidence · 3 forks carry it*

Departmental cargo orders arrive shrink-wrapped in a coloured tamper seal keyed to whoever paid for them, so a cargo tech's job becomes hauling the crate to the right department rather than dumping it in the lobby: when someone from that department opens the seal, the deliverer is paid a bounty in spesos, and someone ripping it off by hand or cutting it open instead gets the deliverer fined and the buyer refunded. If a station keeps breaking seals, the Interstellar Trade Guild sends a station-wide announcement telling command to look into whoever is handling their orders. Alongside that, cargo gets roughly three dozen extra order options (armoury, atmos, engineering, livestock, novelty, mail trolleys and bags), bulk 1000-mol gas orders including chilled liquid variants, a pallet that buys and sells gas straight through connected pipes instead of by the canister, and a handheld Mail Companion that scans a letter or parcel and relays the recipient's live suit-sensor coordinates on a countdown before needing to recalibrate.

- **Take** — It turns cargo from a vending machine into an actual courier job with per-delivery pay, a fine for cutting corners, and a station-wide reputation that command hears about.
- **Skip** — Tamper seals wrap every departmental order, so you are retuning how fast every department on the station gets its supplies, not just adding a cargo minigame, and the payout/fine loop assumes the fork's department-account and seal-on-spawn wiring rather than sitting beside it.
- **Touches** — cargo, atmospherics, engineering, medical, security, science, service, command, all-players
- **Needs** — [mail-delivery](#mail-delivery), [exotic-gas-expansion](#exotic-gas-expansion)
- **Verified** — supported. SharedTamperSealValueSystem.OnSealOpened/OnSealDestroyed calls TryAdjustBankAccount(bank, mutation.Account, ...) against a per-department "Accounts" dictionary (Cargo/Engineering/Medical/Science/Security/Service) with RevenueDistribution and PrimaryCut/LockboxCut fields. I fetched Content.Shared/Cargo/Components/StationBankAccountComponent.cs directly (an upstream-namespaced path, not under _Starlight) and it already contains this multi-account dictionary structure baked in — meaning the Starlight fork's own repo has rewritten a genuinely upstream file to support the department-account model the seal reward/fine loop requires. That confirms the claim's 'needs-upstream-edits' call and specifically proves the fork-patches-upstream reading: the path-data's 'zero files outside fork namespace' signal was blind to this in-place edit, exactly as the seed_means note warned.

**funky**

*loop-change · needs upstream edits · medium confidence · 3 forks carry it*

Bounties stop being a random grab-bag and start arriving as themed department orders: botany gets asked for fifteen carrots or a dozen galaxythistle, the bar gets asked for 90 units of a specific cocktail, and other pools ask for reagents or bottled gas, each with its own quantity band and per-unit payout, so the people who actually make the thing are the ones being paid to make it. Atmos gets its own wallet ("Atmospheric Integrity Reserves") and a Gas Reserves tab on the cargo console where someone buys moles of a chosen gas by the speso, sets an extraction rate and a pressure ceiling, or flips on auto-buy so the station keeps topping itself up, with every purchase announced over engineering radio naming the buyer, the gas and the account. Salvagers spend salvage tickets at their own vendor on spationaut and mining hardsuits, upgrade kits and a single one-of-a-kind Maxim suit, and haulers move goods around in wheeled cargo carts that visibly stack up to four big cardboard supply boxes.

- **Take** — Category-based bounties turn cargo's payout loop into per-department work orders, which gives botany, the bar and medical a steady reason to talk to cargo instead of cargo grinding alone.
- **Skip** — It is three loosely related reworks in one bundle: the gas-reserves console assumes a purchasable-atmos economy and hooks a new tab into the cargo console, and the salvage ticket vendor is worthless without whatever hands out salvage tickets, so grafting the bounty categories alone means unpicking the rest.
- **Touches** — cargo, salvage, engineering, atmospherics, service, botany, medical
- **Verified** — partly supported. Fetched the two cited files that most plausibly touch shared systems and found direct, non-hypothetical evidence the fork edits upstream-owned files in place: Content.Shared/Cargo/Prototypes/CargoBountyPrototype.cs (namespace Content.Shared.Cargo.Prototypes, MIT header, otherwise-upstream file) has CargoReagentBountyItemEntry/CargoGasBountyItemEntry appended under a "// End of Funky Station edits" marker, and Content.Client/Cargo/UI/CargoConsoleMenu.xaml.cs has "// Funkystation: Gas extractor controls" hooks wiring in a _Funkystation.Cargo.UI.GasExtractorTabContent widget. Neither file appears in the unit's own evidence_cited list (which only lists _Funkystation-namespaced files), confirming path-data blindness to in-place upstream edits exactly as seed_means warned — this downgrades the drop-in seed and the claim's own needs-upstream-edits/fork-patches-upstream framing turns out to be the correct one, not merely a cautious guess.

The only `gas: Tritium` example in bountyCategories.yml is commented out (`#`) as authoring-template text, not a live category, so 'bottled gas' bounties are not actually shipped in the evidence provided.

**ephemeral-space, gaby-station-now-dumont-station, goobstation, impstation, monolith, serbia-strong, sunrise**

*activity · needs upstream edits · medium confidence · 3 forks carry it*

Mostly this is more stuff to buy and more stuff to hunt down. Several forks bolt extra pages onto the cargo order catalog (armory, food, fun, materials, medical, hydroponics, ship ammo, armor plates) and add their own pools of bounties, so the bounty board keeps throwing new fetch jobs at the crew with written-out flavour requests: send us muffins for our apology service, send us insulated gloves, grow pyrotton for a picky pet. Monolith adds separate pirate and Soviet bounty boards that pay for looted faction hardsuits, ship turrets and bluespace drives, and Sunrise adds tiered salvage jobs that pay salvagers for hauling back specific expedition loot. The one real system here is Ephemeral Space's supply request computer: any department can type a request into a console, it lands in a queue cargo can see, and the requester watches its tag move through Pending, In Progress, Completed, Cancelled or Denied, with a searchable warehouse manifest computer showing what is actually sitting on the storeroom pallets. Impstation also prints a paper invoice with each delivered order naming the item, who requested it, which account paid, who approved it and why.

- **Take** — The bounty pools and catalog pages are pure YAML content that gives cargo and salvage more to do all round without touching how anything already works, and Ephemeral's request console finally gives non-cargo departments a real channel to ask for things instead of shouting on radio.
- **Skip** — Almost every bounty and catalog entry points at entities, tags and sprites the donor fork already has, so a graft is a long tail of missing-prototype errors, and the Monolith pirate board is unusable without that fork's ship-combat content; the request console and printed invoices are the only parts that are real systems and they need console prototypes on your maps plus hooks into the upstream order flow.
- **Touches** — cargo, salvage, command, all-players, antagonist
- **Verified** — partly supported. I fetched all 8 cited files plus follow-up browsing. Specific gameplay claims check out closely: ES's requests.ftl has the exact status set (Pending/In Progress/Completed/Cancelled/Denied) plus per-department request consoles and a Master console (verified in computers.yml, which shows the whole thing is a self-contained _ES component/BUI/circuit-board stack, not a patch to a vanilla console); storeroom.ftl confirms the searchable warehouse manifest. Impstation's invoice.ftl has exactly Item/Requested by/Payer+accountcode/Approved by/Reason. Impstation's bounties.ftl has the muffins-for-apology-service and insulated-gloves flavor text verbatim. Monolith's pirate-bounties.ftl confirms faction hardsuits, GCS ship turrets, and a bluespace drive; browsing the fork's cargo locale folder turned up a second file, ussp-bounties.ftl, confirming the claimed separate 'Soviet' (USSP) bounty board that wasn't even in the cited evidence list. Sunrise's salvage_jobs.yml confirms tiered (Tier2/Tier3) bounties keyed to fork-specific expedition tags/sprites. The one overclaim is the generic catalog-category list, which reaches past what the cited files show. On graft shape: every evidence file and everything I found by browsing lives under a fork namespace (_ES, _Impstation, _Mono, _Gabystation, _Sunrise) — none patches an upstream directory — so 'fork-patches-upstream' is false. But the ES console architecture (its own component, BUI keys, circuit boards) and fork-specific tags/sprites (e.g. Sunrise's SovietDamagedIDCardExped tag, Monolith's GCS/pirate-faction items) mean using this elsewhere needs new map placements and upstream wiring, matching 'integration-would-require-upstream-edits', not a clean drop-in.

Armory, food, fun, materials, medical, and hydroponics catalog pages are asserted but not backed by any of the 8 cited files for this unit.
