### Player banking and economy

<a id="player-economy-and-banking"></a>

Per-character bank accounts with an in-character currency, ATMs, ID-card balances, salaries, price fluctuation and PDA banking apps that the rest of the fork's commerce feeds off. Scope is money a character earns and spends inside the round. Out-of-round entitlements bought with real money or granted by tier belong to `sponsor-and-donator-perks`; linking a player to a Discord account belongs to `discord-and-external-services`.

**forky**

*activity · needs upstream edits · medium confidence · 4 forks carry it*

This adds physical money-substitute props and one new precious material rather than any account or salary system. Players get poker chips that stack and visibly change appearance as denominations, spawning in fixed piles from 5 up to 100,000, described in-game as "not worth real money but good for representing it" — so a bartender or a bored assistant can run a casino table with something that actually looks like a pot. Alongside them are metal hydrogen ingots: a shiny stackable material worth roughly $250 a unit that piles up to thirty, can be ground for hydrogen, and mostly exists as a high-value thing to hoard, sell or trade.

- **Take** — Poker chips are a tiny, cheap prop that unlocks player-run gambling with the card decks the game already has, and they cost nothing to maintain.
- **Skip** — There is no banking here at all — the chips carry no rules of their own and only mean something by player convention, and the metal hydrogen half is orphaned without the fork's atmos gas expansion that produces it.
- **Touches** — service, cargo, engineering, all-players
- **Needs** — [exotic-gas-expansion](#exotic-gas-expansion)
- **Verified** — supported. Every specific in the gameplay text checks out against the raw files: pokerchips.yml has PokerChipBase through PokerChip100000 with layerStates/thresholds at 5,10,25,50,100,250,500,1000 and the description text "Not worth real money but good for representing it in lieu of it." ingots.yml/metals.yml/metal.yml confirm MetalHydrogen is Extractable (grinds to Hydrogen reagent), stacks to maxCount 30, and carries the dev comment "price: 2.50 # $250 for 1 unit" verbatim matching the claim's $250 figure. Crucially, going beyond the cited evidence paths, I found the fork's own vending inventory Resources/Prototypes/Catalog/VendingMachines/Inventories/games.yml (NOT under _Funkystation) contains "PokerChip10000: 10 #Funky Change - I have a gambling addiction" wired into the vanilla VendingMachineGames ("Good Clean Fun") machine in Resources/Prototypes/Entities/Structures/Machines/vending_machines.yml. That is a genuine in-place edit of an upstream-namespaced file the path-data evidence list never cited, which independently proves the claim's downgrade from the seed's "drop-in" to "needs-upstream-edits" was correct. The depends_on claim (exotic-gas-expansion) is also directly confirmed: Atmospherics/reactions.yml defines MetalHydrogenReaction requiring hydrogen/bz gas mixes that only exist because of the fork's exotic gas set.

**monolith**

*loop-change · entangled · medium confidence · 4 forks carry it*

Money on Monolith moves in two layers. Inside the round, prices are not fixed: a set of tradeable goods carries a market value that wanders every second and slowly pulls back toward a base worth, so a crew hauling cargo to a sell pad can get noticeably more or less for the same haul depending on when they sell, and hoarding to wait out a dip becomes a real call. Selling certain items also skims a cut into (or out of) the sector's department budgets, and anything you bought from a vending machine only fetches half price if you dump it back on the same ship it came from, closing the buy-low-sell-high loop on your own vendors. Outside the round, each player account carries a persistent savings balance shown in the UI as "Account savings: $N" that survives between rounds and can be granted or transferred by staff. There are also two new fabrication stations, an Arc Furnace and a Precision Assembler, with their own recipe lists in the guidebook, plus expanded pirate and USSP bounty boards paying out for hardsuits, faction weapons and other salvaged gear.

- **Take** — Drifting prices alone turn cargo selling from a fixed-rate chore into a timing decision, and it is a small, self-contained component plus one system that anyone running a cargo loop could feel immediately.
- **Skip** — It is not one feature but a bundle sitting on borrowed foundations: the tax component reaches into Frontier's vendored sector bank accounts, the persistent savings balance needs new database tables and server DB methods, the vending resale rule has to be called from the cargo pallet pricing path, and Monolith's own economy guidebook page still says the content is not implemented yet.
- **Touches** — cargo, command, all-players, antagonist
- **Needs** — [cross-fork-vendored-bundles](#cross-fork-vendored-bundles), [cargo-bounties-and-market](#cargo-bounties-and-market), [vending-and-loot-catalogs](#vending-and-loot-catalogs)
- **Verified** — partly supported. The claim's graft_shape is already "entangled" (a downgrade from the drop-in seed), and re-fetching the evidence confirms that downgrade is correct — if anything it understates the entanglement. ItemTaxComponent (Content.Shared/_Mono/Cargo/ItemTaxComponent.cs) literally imports Content.Shared._NF.Bank.Components and keys its TaxAccounts dictionary on the SectorBankAccount enum defined in Content.Server/_NF/Bank/SectorBankComponent.cs, a Frontier-vendored bundle. More importantly, cloning the repo and grepping showed the fork's own copies of upstream files are edited in place with '// Mono' tags to wire this feature in: Content.Server/Cargo/Systems/PricingSystem.cs adds a VendingMachinePurchaseSystem dependency and a GetStaticPriceWithVendingDiscount method, Content.Server/VendingMachines/VendingMachineSystem.cs adds the same dependency, and Content.Server/Cargo/Systems/CargoSystem.Shuttle.cs checks TryComp<ItemTaxComponent> and switches on SectorBankAccount.BlackMarket/Frontier/Nfsd directly in the base cargo-sale path. These are non-_Mono, non-namespaced files the fork patches directly (fork-patches-upstream in spirit), not merely files that would need future upstream edits to integrate — so this unit sits well past 'needs-upstream-edits' into genuinely entangled/bundled territory, matching the claim's depends_on list (cross-fork-vendored-bundles, cargo-bounties-and-market). Separately, the persistent-savings half of the feature (MonoCoinsManager, ServerDbBase MonoCoins methods, currency:add / currency:transfer / currency:balance console commands) is real, DB-backed, and matches the described UI text and admin/staff grant capability.
  - unsupported: "a set of tradeable goods carries a market value that wanders every second and slowly pulls back toward a base worth, so a crew hauling cargo to a sell pad can get noticeably more or less for the same haul depending on when they sell, and hoarding to wait out a dip becomes a real call" — the drift math is real (DriftingPriceSystem/DriftingPriceComponent genuinely mean-reverts toward BasePrice), but a full-repo grep for DriftingPriceComponent/DriftingPrice across Resources/Prototypes shows it is attached to exactly four entities: BaseBitcoin and its three variants (Contribcoin, Ideascoin, Goidacoin) in Resources/Prototypes/_Mono/Entities/Objects/Misc/bitcoin.yml — novelty collectible items worth $8,000-$30,000 each. It is not wired to ore, minerals, or any general cargo/trade good, so 'a crew hauling cargo to a sell pad... for the same haul' misrepresents a niche collectible-flip mechanic as a core cargo-economy feature.
  - unsupported: "expanded pirate and USSP bounty boards paying out for hardsuits, faction weapons and other salvaged gear" — Resources/Prototypes/_Mono/Catalogs/Bounties/ussp_bounties.yml contains bounties for artifacts, bread, soup, pizza, and vodka; a full grep of that file for hardsuit/weapon/faction returns zero hits. Only pirate_bounties.yml pays out for hardsuits and faction weapons (PirateBountyTacsuit, PirateBountyTSFEnergyWeapon, etc.); the USSP board is not part of that reward pattern.
  - unsupported: (from claim_to_refute.skip_because) "Monolith's own economy guidebook page still says the content is not implemented yet" — a full clone of the repo and grep across Resources/ServerInfo/_Mono/Guidebook/ (Economy.xml, Basics.xml, ArcFurnace.xml, PrecisionAssembler.xml, EconomyRecipes.xml, and Misc.xml) for 'not implemented', 'unimplemented', 'WIP', 'coming soon', 'placeholder' returns zero matches; the guidebook pages read as complete, populated content.

**backmen**

*loop-change · needs upstream edits · medium confidence · 4 forks carry it*

Every character starts the round with a personal bank account tied to their ID card, complete with an account number, a PIN and a balance in station credits. You walk up to an ATM, insert your card, punch in your PIN and see "Welcome, <name>! Balance: 4200¢", then withdraw physical cash notes in denominations from 10 up to a million. Shopkeepers, bartenders and department stalls carry a handheld EFTPOS terminal: they punch in a price, you swipe your ID, and the money moves from your account to theirs without any cash changing hands, and each department (cargo, medical, security, science, command, civilian) has its own pre-linked terminal and account. Wages land automatically on a payday timer roughly every half hour, and a wage console lets command staff see a row per crewmember, edit what each one is paid and hand out one-off bonuses. Admins can mint an account for a card or look up its PIN and balance through a right-click trick verb.

- **Take** — It is a complete, playable money loop rather than a stub: personal accounts, PIN-protected ATMs, cash notes, card-swipe payment terminals and an automatic payroll with a command-side wage console, which is everything a fork needs to make a service or merchant playstyle actually mean something.
- **Skip** — It does not stay in its own namespace: ID cards carry a stored bank account number, the uplink/store purchase path is rewired to draw from bank balances, and the player-facing bank app is a PDA cartridge that lives outside these files, so grafting it means patching upstream ID and store code and bringing companion fork systems along. Much of the surfaced text is untranslated Russian, so a fork would also own a localisation pass and ongoing upkeep as upstream's store and ID systems move.
- **Touches** — cargo, command, service, all-players, antagonist
- **Needs** — [pda-cartridge-programs](#pda-cartridge-programs)
- **Verified** — supported. Every specific in the gameplay description checks out against the actual repo: atm.ftl has the exact welcome/balance/PIN strings, eftpos.yml defines per-department preset terminals (cargo/civilian/command/engineering/medical/security/science/specific) each linked to its own account, cargo_cash.yml has denominations 10 through 1,000,000, WageSchedulerSystem.cs has a literal 1800s (30 min) payout interval, and EconomySystem.cs's admin trick-verb mints accounts and reveals PIN/balance exactly as described (with the hardcoded untranslated-Russian strings the claim flags). The wage console's row-per-crewmember/edit-pay/bonus behavior isn't in the cited evidence_cited list but is real — I found and read the companion WageConsoleSystem.cs (not cited) which implements OnEditWageRow and OnBonusMsg exactly as claimed. Critically, I fetched Content.Shared/Access/Components/IdCardComponent.cs (upstream, non-Backmen path) and confirmed it now carries a `storedBankAccountNumber` DataField, and Content.Server/Store/Systems/StoreSystem.Ui.cs (upstream) now calls `HandleBankTransaction` — both are genuine in-place edits to upstream files, which the path-data-only seed could not see. This proves the claim's downgrade from 'drop-in' to 'needs-upstream-edits' is correct, and settles upstream_reading as 'both': the fork's own copy really does patch upstream files (fork-patches-upstream), and grafting it elsewhere would independently require the same kind of upstream wiring (integration-would-require-upstream-edits).

**frontier**

*structural · needs upstream edits · high confidence · 4 forks carry it*

Every character gets a personal "NT Galactic Bank" account holding spesos, which follows them for the whole shift instead of living in the cash in their pockets. You walk up to a bank ATM to check your balance, feed in cash to deposit it, or withdraw a stack of bills to hand to another player, and the same account is what pays when you buy from a vending machine or place a cargo order, so a machine can advertise that it charges or pays out above or below market rate. There is also a station-side terminal where authorised crew move money in and out of organisation accounts (Frontier Station, the sheriff's department) and must tag each transaction with a reason such as payroll, work order, supplies, bounty, fines or donation, and those accounts tick up on their own over time and produce an income-and-expenses ledger printout at the end of the round.

- **Take** — It is the money layer every other commerce feature can hang off: once characters have persistent balances and stations have tagged treasury accounts, vending, cargo, bounties, salaries and player-to-player trade all become one connected economy instead of loose cash piles.
- **Skip** — The bank is only worth anything if you also rework the things that spend money — vending machines, cargo consoles, stores — to bill against balances, so the graft drags a chain of upstream purchase-path edits behind it, and on a station round where nobody needs to earn a living it mostly adds an ATM chore.
- **Touches** — cargo, command, security, service, all-players
- **Verified** — partly supported. Fetched all six cited files plus VendingMachineSystem.cs and the Cargo system files. The personal-account, ATM deposit/withdraw, market-rate modifier, sector-account withdrawal-reason tags, and end-of-round ledger claims are all directly confirmed in the fetched .ftl/.xml/.yml/.cs files. But the claim that "the same account... pays when you buy from a vending machine or place a cargo order" is only half right: vending purchases genuinely draw on the personal BankAccountComponent (confirmed in Content.Server/VendingMachines/VendingMachineSystem.cs), while cargo orders (CargoSystem.Orders.cs) draw on the separate, upstream-vanilla per-department StationBankAccountComponent, not the personal player bank — these are two distinct account systems that happen to share the word "bank." The needs-upstream-edits graft_shape is directly confirmed: VendingMachineSystem.cs, a file in the plain upstream Content.Server/VendingMachines directory (not under _NF), has been edited in place with `// Frontier` markers to add a BankSystem dependency and a TryBankWithdraw() call, proving the fork's own copy patches upstream files rather than staying confined to _NF namespaces.
  - unsupported: the same account is what pays when you buy from a vending machine or place a cargo order — cargo orders are actually paid from the separate, upstream-vanilla per-station-department StationBankAccountComponent (Cargo/Engineering/Medical/Science/Security/Service funds), not from the personal player Bank account that vending machines draw on

**funky, gaby-station-now-dumont-station, goobstation, serbia-strong, starlight, white-dream**

*loop-change · needs upstream edits · medium confidence · 4 forks carry it*

Your character gets a bank balance and a paycheck: a salary lands in your account every so often with a chat notice ("Salary credited, 240 cr."), and you walk up to a wall or freestanding ATM to check your balance, feed cash in (10% deposit fee), pull cash back out, or wire money to another crewmate by name. Prices on shop goods are rerolled each round inside per-category bands (a drink is 1-10 cr, a basic tool 10-30), so the same sandwich costs a different amount shift to shift. Around the edges the same bucket adds bar-and-casino props to spend it on: slot machines, a coin flipper and a claw machine, stackable poker chips, and a break-glass "money cabinet" on the wall holding 2500 spesos for emergencies. Two of the six forks here are only loosely economy at all: Goob's currency is an out-of-round wallet spent on antag/hat tokens, and White Dream's entry is playtime-unlocked ghost sprites.

- **Take** — A personal balance plus a recurring paycheck gives every crewmate a reason to care about money, which is what makes bartenders, botanists and cargo actually tradeable roles instead of free-vending-machine roles.
- **Skip** — Starlight's salary path is wired into its NullLink external player-data service rather than to anything in-round, and making randomized prices matter means tagging a lot of upstream item prototypes with a price category, so the "drop-in" impression does not survive contact.
- **Touches** — all-players, cargo, service, command, ghost-roles
- **Needs** — [discord-and-external-services](#discord-and-external-services)
- **Verified** — supported. Every concrete detail in the gameplay text checks out against the actual files. Starlight's atm-ui.ftl reads verbatim "economy-chat-salary-message = Salary credited, {$amount} cr." and states withdrawal is 0% fee / deposit is 10% fee, matching the claim exactly; price_categories.yml has drink min:1/max:10 and tool_basic min:10/max:30, matching the claim's numbers precisely; Gabystation's atm.yml shows both a freestanding ComputerBankATM and a ComputerWallmountBankATM with cash/card slots; Funkystation's pokerchips.yml is a stackable Stack item and money_cabinet.yml is filled with SpaceCash2500 behind a FireAxeCabinet-style lock; Goobstation's token_listings.yml is literally HighTierAntagToken/AdminAbuseToken/HatToken (out-of-round, not banking); White Dream's custom-ghosts-ui.ftl is playtime-gated ghost cosmetics, not economy. ### Mail delivery

<a id="mail-delivery"></a>

Addressed parcels arriving on a timer for a mail carrier to deliver to the right recipient for payout, with per-department contents and tampering as a crime.

**funky**

*activity · needs upstream edits · medium confidence · 4 forks carry it*

Parcels that arrive on the station are no longer generic boxes: there are small letters, big cartons and flat parcels, some stamped fragile, some taped as priority, some locked so only the addressee's ID opens them, and some marked with a radiation hazard symbol. What is inside is written for the recipient's job, so a chemist's crate holds jugs of hydrogen or sugar, a paramedic gets a roller bed, the chaplain gets candles, the bartender gets shakers and beanbag shells, and the joke deliveries range from spam letters and a carton of eggs to a closet that coughs up a skeleton or a flashbang taped to a live gorilla. To haul it all around there is a wheeled mailcart you push through the halls, with visible slots that fill up on the sprite as you load large, flat and small parcels onto it.

- **Take** — It turns an already-shipped upstream system from a trickle of generic boxes into a large, department-flavoured parcel catalogue with a mailcart to move it, all in fork-namespaced YAML with no C# of its own.
- **Skip** — The parcel contents name dozens of specific item prototypes (premium spirits, infinite candles, emergency roller beds, gag papers) that a fork may not have, so a graft is a long tail of missing-prototype fixes plus wiring the new parcels into the mail delivery pool and importing the mail and mailcart sprite sheets; it also permanently ties your loot table to Funky's item list.
- **Touches** — cargo, service, medical, science, security, engineering, all-players
- **Needs** — [vending-and-loot-catalogs](#vending-and-loot-catalogs)
- **Verified** — supported; assessed as drop-in, corrected by the verifier. The six cited _Funkystation YAML files check out gameplay-wise (fragile/priority/locked/radioactive stamps, job/department-flavored contents for Chemist/Medical/Chaplain/Bartender, joke parcels, wheeled mailcart with fillable slots — all read directly from source, including the exact addressee-ID-lock mechanism in MailSystem.cs). But the \"drop-in\" call is wrong: every cited entity parents off BaseMail, which lives in Resources/Prototypes/Nyanotrasen/Entities/Objects/Specific/Mail/base_mail.yml, backed by Content.Server/Content.Shared/Content.Client \"Nyanotrasen\"-namespaced Mail C#, and the actual job-weighted delivery pool that makes these new parcels reachable in play sits in Resources/Prototypes/_Goobstation/Mail/mailDeliveries.yml — none of that is under _Funkystation or in the evidence list. Worse, checking honksquad-ss14's own tree directly shows it has no BaseMail/Mail component anywhere; it already runs the newer, renamed upstream \"Delivery\" system (Content.Shared/Delivery/DeliveryComponent.cs et al.), so this isn't a same-system prototype gap — it's two incompatible parcel-delivery architectures that would need to be reconciled.
  - unsupported: "all in fork-namespaced YAML with no C# of its own" (take_because) — the parcels depend on a substantial pre-existing Mail component/system (MailComponent, MailSystem, MailTeleporterComponent, StationMailRouterComponent, MailDeliveryPoolPrototype, MailVisuals, plus a client-side MailComponent/MailSystem) and the root BaseMail abstract entity, none of which live under _Funkystation and none of which are in evidence_cited.
  - unsupported: graft_shape: "drop-in" — refuted. BaseMail (the parent every cited entity chains up to) is defined at Resources/Prototypes/Nyanotrasen/Entities/Objects/Specific/Mail/base_mail.yml, and the job/department weight table that actually wires these Funky-authored parcels into deliveries (mailDeliveryPool: BaseMailDeliveryPool) lives at Resources/Prototypes/_Goobstation/Mail/mailDeliveries.yml — both outside _Funkystation and outside the cited evidence.
  - unsupported: skip_because's "wiring the new parcels into the mail delivery pool" understates the real cost: honksquad-ss14 has no BaseMail/MailComponent/MailSystem at all in its current tree — it already ships the renamed, incompatible upstream `Delivery` system (Content.Shared/Delivery/DeliveryComponent.cs, DeliverySpawnerComponent, etc.), so a graft means reconciling with or replacing an entire pre-existing parallel architecture, not just adding entries to an existing pool.

**forky**

*cosmetic · drop-in · high confidence · 4 forks carry it*

Forky's contribution here is a second set of station tubes just for mail: chunky yellow-ish pipe segments, bends, junctions, taggers and routers (including a signal-controlled one) that look distinct from the grey garbage disposal tubes but work the same way, and can be built out of two steel sheets a piece and cut back down with a welder. In play it means a parcel dropped into a mail trunk travels its own visibly separate line across the station instead of sharing the trash chutes, and an engineer or cargo tech can tag and route packages to a specific department outlet. There is no new mail parcel, mail machine or carrier job in this content, only the tube network itself.

- **Take** — It is 36 sprites and two YAML files with zero code, and it cleanly separates mail routing from garbage disposal visually so a mail tube run across a map reads as mail rather than trash.
- **Skip** — Every entity just re-parents the upstream disposal pipes with new sprites, so it adds no behaviour at all, and the fork ships only the construction graph, not a construction menu recipe or any mail machine to plug into it, so you would have to supply the actual mail delivery gameplay yourself.
- **Touches** — cargo, service, engineering
- **Verified** — partly supported. Both cited files (mailpiping.yml, mailpipes.yml) are entirely within _Funkystation namespaces and I found no other file in the repo tree referencing MailPipe/MailTagger/MailTrunk/MailRouter/etc. Every entity only overrides Sprite and Construction on top of an upstream `parent:` (DisposalPipe, DisposalTagger, DisposalTrunk, DisposalRouter, DisposalJunction, DisposalYJunction, DisposalBend, DisposalSignalRouter), so it inherits vanilla disposal behavior unchanged — confirming \"work the same way\" and \"adds no behaviour.\" The construction graph confirms the 2-steel-sheet build and weld-to-deconstruct claims exactly, and I confirmed (matching upstream's own disposal.yml pattern) there is no top-level `type: construction` menu recipe anywhere in the repo referencing the `mailpipes` graph, so \"no construction menu recipe\" is accurate. The repo-wide search also shows vanilla SS14 already ships a full mail system (MailingUnit, mail_teleporter, mail_bag, mailbox, mail.rsi parcels) untouched by Funky, so \"no new mail parcel, mail machine, or carrier job\" is correct and the whole unit is a real drop-in — its only dependency is on core vanilla disposal prototypes any SS14-derived target already has. The one hard factual defect is the color: the sprites are blue, not yellow-ish, and the sprite count is off by one.
  - unsupported: "chunky yellow-ish pipe segments" — the actual mailpipes.rsi sprites (conpipe-s.png, conpipe-tagger.png, conpipe-t.png, pipe-s.png, etc.) render in dark navy/steel blue, not yellow or yellow-ish. Direct pixel comparison against upstream disposal.rsi/conpipe-s.png confirms disposal pipes are grey and mail pipes are blue — the "looks distinct from grey disposal tubes" half of the claim holds, but the specific color named is wrong.
  - unsupported: "It is 36 sprites" — the mailpipes.rsi folder contains 35 PNG state images (verified via meta.json states list and GitHub directory listing), not 36. Only reaches 36 if the meta.json itself is miscounted as a sprite.

**impstation**

*activity · needs upstream edits · medium confidence · 4 forks carry it*

Mail still arrives in shipments at the telepad with an announcement ("A new shipment has arrived! Next shipment in approximately X minutes"), but what is inside a parcel now depends on who it is addressed to: the game checks for a table specific to that person's job first, then their department, then falls back to the generic pool. The pool of things people can receive is much wider and sillier than the default: books and holy texts, snacks, toys, small live creatures, fancy pens, bouquets, joints, cigarettes, hormone syringes, cap guns, knives, light and bike-horn implanters, instruments, bongs, cosplay outfits and novelty kits like a contract-killer's backpack or a homunculus chemistry set. Two extras ride along: any item marked as "mailinatable" gets a right-click "Send to nearest Mail Telepad" option that takes five seconds and teleports it with a beam effect and a departure/arrival chime (or tells you there is nothing in range), and some parcels hold a placeholder that only becomes the real thing when you take it out or drop it, so opening certain mail sets off whatever was packed inside.

- **Take** — Job- and department-aware mail turns a generic parcel into a small piece of characterisation for the recipient, and the loot tables are pure YAML you can repopulate with your own fork's items without touching the logic.
- **Skip** — The headline feature is unfinished on the source side: both DepartmentalLetters and DepartmentalPackages ship with empty departmentTables/jobTables and a comment telling you to populate them, so you would be grafting a routing mechanism plus a pile of authoring work, and the routing itself patches the upstream Delivery system rather than sitting in fork-only files.
- **Touches** — cargo, service, all-players
- **Needs** — [reagent-and-reaction-expansion](#reagent-and-reaction-expansion)
- **Verified** — supported. Fetched all 9 cited files plus the upstream DeliveryComponent.cs they patch. Every specific claim checks out: mail.ftl has the exact announcement string quoted; deliveries.yml's comment block spells out the job->primary-department->fallback-department->generic priority order verbatim and both DepartmentalLetters/DepartmentalPackages entities really do ship with empty departmentTables/jobTables and 'TODO: Populate this' comments; deliveries_items.yml and deliveries_tables.yml contain the contract-killer backpack, hormone syringes (testosterone/estradiol), homunculus kit, books (RandomBookTable) + HolyTextEntityTable, bouquets, joints, knives, light/bike-horn implanters, instruments, bongs, cosplay kits, small creatures (MobSlug/MobBee/etc) and toys exactly as described; MailinatorSystem.cs/Component.cs confirm the alt-verb 'Send to nearest Mail Telepad', 5-second DoAfter, beam VFX and departure/arrival sounds; DelayedItemComponent.cs is literally the placeholder-that-becomes-real-item-on-drop mechanism described. Crucially, DeliverySystem.Spawns.cs is a partial class declared in the upstream namespace (Content.Server.Delivery) and its logic reads DepartmentTables/JobTables off DeliveryComponent -- and fetching Content.Shared/Delivery/DeliveryComponent.cs (an upstream path, not under _Impstation/) shows those two dictionary fields were added directly inside the original file between '// IMP start' / '// IMP end' markers. That is a genuine in-place edit of an upstream file, confirming needs-upstream-edits over the path-data drop-in seed and settling the ambiguous phrase toward fork-patches-upstream.

**monolith, starlight, sunrise, the-den**

*activity · needs upstream edits · medium confidence · 4 forks carry it*

On top of the mail parcels the base game already delivers, these forks each bolt on something small. Monolith stuffs extra parcels with things nobody should be mailing: an SMG with three mags, an AK, a bundle of C4, an RCD kit, a double energy sword, and an ERT mail-carrier outfit with 20,000 spesos, so opening a package that landed in your department is occasionally a much bigger deal than a pen and a candy bar. Starlight adds junk mail, propaganda letters urging you to defect to the Syndicate or just start stealing from your coworkers, complete with a line to sign, plus a handheld companion the carrier can use to ping a recipient's suit sensor and get about a minute of tracking on where that person actually is before it goes on cooldown. The Den runs the older Nyanotrasen-style mail instead, where each parcel is locked to a named crewmember and their job, some are marked fragile or priority with a delivery timer, and cargo's account gains on a good delivery or loses money if the box is smashed or arrives late.

- **Take** — Starlight's recipient tracker fixes the real pain of the mail carrier role, actually finding the person the parcel is addressed to, and the spam letters are cheap flavour that gives every crewmember something to read and react to.
- **Skip** — Monolith's contribution is essentially "guns and C4 now arrive in the post", which hands free weapons to whoever happens to open the box and needs a balance decision rather than a copy-paste; The Den's version is a whole parallel mail implementation that would fight the upstream one rather than sit beside it.
- **Touches** — cargo, service, all-players
- **Verified** — partly supported. I fetched all five cited files directly and they check out: Monolith's _Mono/Mail/mail.yml really does contain the SMG+3 mags, AK+3 mags, C4 x3, RCD/RPD kit, double energy sword, and the ERT mail-carrier outfit + 20,000 spesos. Starlight's delivery-spam.ftl really has a "sign here" Syndicate-defection letter and a "steal from your coworkers" letter, and MailCompanionComponent.cs really implements a 1-minute suit-sensor tracker with a cooldown. The Den's MailComponent.cs really has Recipient/RecipientJob/IsLocked/IsFragile/IsPriority/Bounty/Penalty fields matching the "locked to a crewmember, fragile/priority timer, cargo gains or loses money" description. Where the claim falls short is the framing: I traced the actual namespaces (sparse-checkout of all four forks plus upstream space-wizards/master and the honksquad-ss14 target) and found upstream/Starlight/Sunrise run the modern "Delivery" component (Content.Shared/Delivery/*, already present in honksquad-ss14 unmodified), while Monolith and The Den instead carry the older pre-rename "Mail" component (Delta-V/Nyanotrasen lineage) that has no Delivery equivalent in their trees at all. So the "take" piece (Starlight) is genuinely near-drop-in — it only adds _Starlight-namespaced files on top of a Delivery system the target already has — while the "skip" pieces (Monolith, The Den) aren't skippable merely for balance reasons as stated; their YAML/components target an incompatible legacy system that doesn't exist in a Delivery-based target and would need real rework, not a balance call, to port. The Den also places its Server-side files at unprefixed core-looking paths (Content.Server/Mail/Components/MailComponent.cs, no _TheDen/_Nyanotrasen prefix) even though its Shared/Client mirrors are namespaced under Nyanotrasen — a genuine "fork content sitting at unnamespaced paths" pattern, even though no real upstream file exists there to collide with. Separately, Sunrise (one of the 4 forks in the unit) carries zero distinctive mail content, just vanilla Delivery, so "adopted by 4" overstates the contributor count to 3. Net: needs-upstream-edits remains the defensible label for the unit as bundled, but for a more specific and more serious reason (legacy-vs-modern component incompatibility) than the claim's stated "balance decision" framing.
  - unsupported: "On top of the mail parcels the base game already delivers, these forks each bolt on something small." — this frames all four forks as extending the same shared base feature. In fact Monolith and The Den run an older, pre-rename "Mail" component (Nyanotrasen/Delta-V lineage: Content.Server/_DV/Mail/... for Monolith, Content.Server/Mail/... for The Den) that is structurally different from and incompatible with the current upstream "Delivery" system (Content.Shared/Delivery/DeliveryComponent.cs) that Starlight and Sunrise actually use unmodified. Monolith's and The Den's mail is not "on top of" the same feature Starlight sits on — it's a parallel, divergent implementation.

### Shipyard and player-owned ships

<a id="shipyard-player-ships"></a>

A console that sells shuttles from a catalog of hand-mapped hulls, with deeds, ownership records, registration and cleanup for returned vessels.

**backmen, deltav, frontier, impstation, monolith, starlight**

*structural · needs upstream edits · high confidence · 2 forks carry it*

A player pops the ID card out of their PDA, slots it into a shipyard console, and browses a catalogue of complete pre-built shuttles filtered by size, class and engine type: a six-seat private transport, a mobile clinic, a botany barge, a mining prospector, a restaurant ship, and on some forks armed pirate corvettes and black-market hulls. Buy one and it FTLs in and docks, with a deed written onto your ID card that names you its captain and gates the ship's doors and consoles to whoever holds that deed. Dock it back empty with nobody aboard and you can sell it at the console for its appraised value, though it refuses if it sniffs contraband, stolen station equipment, dangerous materials or a pet still on board. Frontier and Monolith add a shuttle records computer that logs every purchase (ship name, buyer, price, whether it's still flying) and lets a crewmate copy the deed onto their own ID for a fee, plus a preview window and a "your ship is 40 meters to the northwest" locator.

- **Take** — It converts a shift from "everyone lives on one station" into "crews own and captain their own vessels," which is the single biggest shape change a fork can make with one console, and it drags a whole ownership/deed/resale economy along with it.
- **Skip** — The console is the cheap part: the value lives in dozens to hundreds of hand-mapped shuttle grids (Frontier ships 240 prototype files, Monolith 394), and grafting the system without building or importing that fleet leaves you an empty catalogue nobody uses.
- **Touches** — cargo, command, security, antagonist, all-players, service, medical
- **Needs** — [player-economy-and-banking](#player-economy-and-banking), [custom-station-maps](#custom-station-maps)
- **Verified** — partly supported. Read ShipyardSystem.cs / ShipyardConsoleSystem.cs / ShipyardConsoleComponent.cs plus full git ls-tree file listings for all six forks (backmen, deltav, frontier, impstation, monolith, starlight): every shipyard-related file in every fork lives under that fork's own namespace directory (_NF, _Mono, _DV, _Starlight, Backmen, _Impstation) with no edits to files outside those directories, so nothing patches upstream in place. But frontier/monolith's variant genuinely depends on a separate fork-only personal bank/economy system (Content.Server._NF.Bank) and on custom shuttle-grid/outpost maps neither of which exist in vanilla, which is a real, confirmed dependency chain matching the claim's downgrade from the seed's drop-in guess.
  - unsupported: "a deed written onto your ID card that names you its captain and gates the ship's doors and consoles to whoever holds that deed" — confirmed only for frontier/monolith (ShuttleDeedComponent, ShipAccessReaderComponent, ship-access-denied locale string). backmen, starlight, deltav and impstation (which literally reuses deltav's Content.Server/_DV/Shipyard/* code wholesale) have no deed/ownership component at all in their shipyard systems — backmen and starlight's only purchase event is ShipyardConsolePurchaseMessage.cs with no Sell/Deed counterpart, and deltav/impstation's ShipyardConsoleSystem.cs just debits a station (not personal) bank account and FTL-docks the grid.
  - unsupported: "Dock it back empty with nobody aboard and you can sell it at the console for its appraised value, though it refuses if it sniffs contraband, stolen station equipment, dangerous materials or a pet still on board" — this full sale/appraisal/contraband-check flow (shipyard-console-sale-organic-aboard, -contraband-onboard, -station-resources, -dangerous-materials, -cute-pets) exists only in frontier/monolith's locale files. deltav's ShipyardSystem.cs and ShipyardConsoleSystem.cs contain zero references to sell, sale, appraisal or deed; backmen and starlight have no sell-related component or event file anywhere in their Shipyard directories.
  - unsupported: "Frontier and Monolith add a shuttle records computer ... plus a preview window and a 'your ship is 40 meters to the northwest' locator" — shuttle-records is genuinely shared (both have Resources/Locale/.../_NF/shuttle-records/shuttle-records-system.ftl), but the preview window (ShipyardPreviewSystem/ShipyardPreviewMenu) and the direction locator (ShipyardDirectionSystem, locale string 'Your {$shipName} is relatively located {$distance} meter(s) to the {$direction}!') exist ONLY under Monolith's own _Mono namespace — a full file-tree listing of new-frontiers-14/frontier-station-14 itself contains no 'direction' or 'preview' file under its Shipyard paths at all. This is a Monolith-only addition on top of NF's shipyard, not a joint Frontier+Monolith feature.
  - unsupported: "a botany barge" — DeltaV's actual catalog has no ship literally combining botany and barge; 'Barge' (id: Barge) is a mining/salvage vessel, and the botanical ship (Eden) is a separate medium vessel categorized Medical, not Botany/Mining. Minor conflation of two distinct ship entries.

### Expedition missions and objectives

<a id="expedition-missions"></a>

Structured off-station runs with typed objectives (capture, rescue, purge, shutdown), mission consoles, rewards and deployable shelters.

**deltav**

*loop-change · needs upstream edits · medium confidence · 5 forks carry it*

Salvagers earn Mining Points by feeding ore into the station's ore processor and smelting it, then tap their ID card on the processor to bank the points to themselves. Those points are the currency for going back out: firing the salvage magnet to haul in another wreck costs a listed number of Mining Points, so the shift becomes a self-funding loop of drag ore home, cash it in, buy the next wreck. Miners also get a voucher they redeem at a vendor for exactly one loadout of their choosing (a kinetic crusher kit, a fulton extraction-and-rescue kit that lets them ship ore and dead bodies home without the shuttle, a survival kit with explorer's webbing and a holoflare gun, a crusher-dagger small arms kit, or a conscription kit that outfits a second crewmember as a miner). Out in the field they can throw down a shelter capsule, which shakes, warns everyone to stand back, and unfolds into a small prefab room on solid ground for a pressurised place to retreat to.

- **Take** — It turns salvage from an open-ended "go get stuff" chore into a closed economic loop where the department funds its own next expedition, which gives miners a concrete score to push and a reason to keep processing ore rather than hoarding it.
- **Skip** — Mining Points are not self-contained: the earning side is bolted onto the upstream lathe (a new recipe field, a print event hook, and a "claim points" button in the lathe UI) and the spending side patches the salvage magnet and ID card prototypes, so grafting it means touching upstream files that will conflict on every sync. The voucher also rides on the thief-backpack set prototype, and several advertised kits (resonator, minebot) are commented-out TODOs upstream in Delta-V itself.
- **Touches** — cargo, salvage, service
- **Verified** — partly supported. Fetched all 9 cited files plus, via Sourcegraph code search, the actual upstream files the claim describes as patched: Content.Shared/Research/Prototypes/LatheRecipePrototype.cs (adds `public uint MiningPoints;` field, line 77), Resources/Prototypes/Entities/Structures/Machines/lathe.yml (OreProcessor entity gets `- type: MiningPoints` and `- type: MiningPointsLathe`, tagged `# DeltaV`), Resources/Prototypes/Recipes/Lathes/sheet.yml (adds `miningPoints: N # DeltaV` to over a dozen smelting recipes), Resources/Prototypes/Entities/Objects/Misc/identification_cards.yml (adds `- type: MiningPoints # DeltaV` to the ID card prototype), Content.Client/Lathe/UI/LatheMenu.xaml(.cs) and LatheBoundUserInterface.cs (adds the claim-points button/label), and Content.Server/Salvage/SalvageSystem.cs + Content.Client/Salvage/UI/SalvageMagnetBoundUserInterface.cs (inject MiningPointsSystem to gate/display the magnet's point cost). None of these are under `_DV/` — they are genuine in-place edits to upstream file paths. This directly contradicts the drop-in seed and confirms the claim's own 'needs-upstream-edits' / 'fork-patches-upstream' assessment; it is not merely a self-contained addition that would need upstream wiring, the fork's actual tree already patches upstream files.
  - unsupported: "then tap their ID card on the processor to bank the points to themselves" — the actual mechanism (MiningPointsSystem.OnClaimMiningPoints, Content.Client/Lathe/UI/LatheMenu.xaml.cs) is a 'claim points' button in the lathe's UI window; pressing it calls SharedIdCardSystem.TryFindIdCard to locate whatever ID the user is already wearing/holding and transfers points to it. There is no physical tap/swipe interaction in the evidence — it's a UI button click, not a card-on-machine interaction.

**frontier**

*loop-change · needs upstream edits · medium confidence · 5 forks carry it*

A crew flies their ship out to open space, uses the salvage console aboard, and picks one of five offered planetside missions, each listing the enemy faction, a time limit, and hazard modifiers like night time, extreme cold, no breathable air, plasma atmosphere, or a rushed clock. The ship jumps to a planet, everyone gets pointed toward an objective building, and they dig and mine through rock, pry open airlocks, fight cultists, xenos, mercenaries or rogue silicons, and haul back ore and loot before the ship jumps home with or without them. Loadout planning is the real game: the console's modifier readout tells you whether to bring a hardsuit, a winter coat, flares, medical supplies, or armour matched to the enemy's damage type, and hostile mobs that chase you off the dungeon grid are killed off so you cannot drag the planet's wildlife home.

- **Take** — It turns salvage from a side errand into a full prep-fight-extract loop with a timer, hazard readouts and enemy variety, giving a whole crew a reason to gear up, coordinate on radio and go somewhere together.
- **Skip** — Frontier's version is built for its ship-owning sector economy (ships bought at the Expeditionary Lodge, telecomms servers aboard, no station radio planetside) and hooks partial-class extensions into upstream mining and salvage systems, so a station-based fork inherits a lot of surrounding assumptions plus ongoing merge pain on upstream salvage files.
- **Touches** — cargo, salvage, mining, medical, security, all-players
- **Needs** — [shipyard-player-ships](#shipyard-player-ships), [hostile-fauna-and-npcs](#hostile-fauna-and-npcs)
- **Verified** — partly supported. Direct evidence of an upstream in-place edit: fetching Content.Shared/Mining/MiningScannerSystem.cs (note: NOT under an _NF directory, unlike the cited MiningScannerSystem.Innate.cs) shows `public sealed partial class MiningScannerSystem : EntitySystem // Frontier: partial` and a call to `NFInitialize(); // Frontier` inside the upstream Initialize() method — the fork literally patched the upstream file to make it partial and wire in the _NF extension. This directly contradicts a drop-in classification and confirms needs-upstream-edits, specifically the fork-patches-upstream reading (not just integration-would-require-upstream-edits).
  - unsupported: hazard modifiers like night time, extreme cold, no breathable air, plasma atmosphere, or a rushed clock — none of the 5 cited evidence files (Expeditions.xml, ore.yml, SalvageMobRestrictionsSystem.cs, EarthDiggingComponent.cs, MiningScannerSystem.Innate.cs) show a modifier list; I could not locate a salvage-mission-modifier prototype/source file to confirm this specific set of hazards

### Lavaland mining planet

<a id="lavaland-mining-planet"></a>

A procedurally generated hostile planet reached by mining shuttle, with ruins, chasms, tendril nests, elite fauna and dedicated miner equipment.

**far-horizons, goobstation**

*loop-change · entangled · medium confidence · 6 forks carry it*

Salvagers board a mining shuttle, punch in a destination on a docking console, and fly down to a hot volcanic planet made of basalt caves: ore-veined rock walls to drill, scattered wrecks and skeleton-strewn ruins holding treasure and salvage loot, bone-armour cult shrines, and nasty surprises like a rocket launcher sitting on a stone table with a hidden turret pointed at whoever grabs it. The planet's thin atmosphere is part of the fight — armour and weapons behave differently at low pressure, so kit that works on-station does not work the same down there. The headline draw is the big monsters: named bosses that telegraph their attacks with glowing warning shapes on the floor so you can read the wind-up and dodge, cycle through named moves (a warning shot that trails each player before dropping, a wide sweep aimed at whoever is furthest away, a flashy spin around itself), spawn healing clones you have to ignore rather than attack, and then shrink the arena for a final showdown once they are nearly dead. Boss music kicks in, and killing one drops upgrade parts you bolt onto your melee weapons and guns.

- **Take** — It gives salvage an actual destination with escalating stakes — a mining planet, readable telegraphed boss fights, and looted weapon upgrades — instead of the station-bound magnet-and-asteroid loop.
- **Skip** — Goob's version is roughly 900 files spanning procedural planet generation, a dedicated shuttle console, a pressure-based combat rules layer, megafauna, and a weapon-upgrade economy; you are adopting a whole department's worth of content and its maintenance burden, not one system, and the Far Horizons boss layer additionally leans on vendored Starlight sprites and its own Abyss faction.
- **Touches** — cargo, salvage, science, ghost-roles, all-players
- **Needs** — [hostile-fauna-and-npcs](#hostile-fauna-and-npcs), [cross-fork-vendored-bundles](#cross-fork-vendored-bundles)
- **Verified** — supported. Every specific gameplay beat I checked was directly backed by real code: elder.yml's BossCombat/mechanics field pointed at elder_boss_mechanics.yml, whose named moves (warning-shot-that-trails-then-drops, furthest-target sweep, self-centered flourish, healing-decoy clones that heal the boss extra when attacked, final-showdown arena shrink at 20% health) match the claim's move-by-move description almost verbatim; bait.yml literally contains a TableStone + WeaponLauncherRocket + WeaponTurretHostile cluster; DockingConsoleSystem.cs implements the FTL docking-console shuttle flow; PressureArmorChangeComponent.cs implements pressure-tiered armor penetration; BossMusicSystem.cs and MeleeUpgradesSystem.cs/MegafaunaWeaponLooterComponent.cs confirm boss music and weapon-upgrade looting. The 'entangled' graft_shape is also confirmed in the code itself: TileChaserSystem.cs depends on the fork's own Anger and Megafauna namespaces, elder.rsi is sprited from a vendored _Starlight/Mobs/Abyss path with an Abyss NPC faction, and the Content.Server/_Lavaland tree spans Procedural, Biome, Megafauna, Weapons, Atmos, Shuttles as separate subsystems — exactly the sprawl the claim describes as the reason to skip it.

## Machines

### Access control rework

<a id="access-control-rework"></a>

Changes how doors and equipment check identity: rebuilt access sets, scan gates, secure terminals, keypad locks, grid ownership and ID-gated item use.

**rmc14**

*loop-change · entangled · medium confidence · 6 forks carry it*

Command staff work an ID terminal that first makes them badge in with their own card, then lets them slot a crewmate's card and re-badge it wholesale: pick a job, and the card instantly gets that role's entire door-and-locker set (UNMC Command, Medical, Engineering, Military Police, Requisitions, the marine squad roles, plus colony and corporate sets), tick individual accesses on top, post someone to a squad, flip their friend-or-foe tag, or "terminate" a card so it stops reading as friendly. Every one of those edits is written into the ship AI's public identification log, so a quiet promotion or a stripped card can be read back later by anyone who checks. Because access is bundled per role, your card is also what decides which equipment vendors will hand you gear, not just which doors open, and wall-mounted keycard stations need two people to swipe authorized cards at separate posts within a short window of each other before the ship will go to Red Alert.

- **Take** — Bundling access into named role groups turns ID editing from tag-by-tag clicking into one meaningful command decision, and the two-person keycard turn plus the public AI log give access changes real social weight.
- **Skip** — It is not a standalone access system: the console reaches into that fork's squad assignment, rank, skill, IFF faction and ship-AI logging systems, and the group tree itself is written around a marine job roster, so porting it means either dragging those in or rewriting most of the prototypes for your own jobs.
- **Touches** — command, security, medical, engineering, cargo, all-players
- **Needs** — [squads-ranks-and-skills](#squads-ranks-and-skills), [extra-job-roster](#extra-job-roster), [firearms-content-expansion](#firearms-content-expansion)
- **Verified** — supported. IdModificationConsoleSystem.cs directly imports and depends on SquadSystem, SharedRankSystem, SkillsSystem, GunIFFSystem, ARESCoreSystem, and Roles/OriginalRoleComponent — every mechanic the claim describes (job-group re-badge, squad assignment, IFF toggle, termination, AI logging) is implemented by calling into these fork-specific systems in the same file. The claim's own graft_shape ('entangled') is well supported and correctly overrides the seed's 'drop-in' path-data guess, which evidently could not see this C#-level coupling.
  - unsupported: "your card is also what decides which equipment vendors will hand you gear" — only indirectly evidenced (a single code comment in marine_access_groups.yml: "this exists because other squad members will have their own equipment vendors"); no vendor-gating system file was found/read to directly confirm access tags drive vendor permissions.
  - unsupported: "written into the ship AI's public identification log ... can be read back later by anyone who checks" — ARESCoreSystem.CreateARESLog and the ARESTabIdentificationLogs category are real and confirmed, but 'public'/'anyone who checks' access scope was inferred from folder names (ExternalTerminals/Tabs) rather than from reading an actual terminal-access-control file.

**serbia-strong**

*loop-change · needs upstream edits · medium confidence · 6 forks carry it*

Some doors only open if you approach them from the right side, so a checkpoint airlock lets people out freely but refuses anyone pushing in from the wrong direction, and certain doors can be gated on what you *are* rather than what your ID says, letting a door open for a borg or a specific faction while rejecting a stolen card. Certain items refuse to be picked up, worn or dragged by the wrong person at all: grab a weapon or piece of gear you're not cleared for and it slips out of your hands with a warning message, a buzz, and in some cases a shock that hurts you for trying. There is also a painter machine with a slot for a PDA and a slot for an ID card that reskins them to look like a different department's, so you can walk around presenting as someone you aren't, and the ID access list itself is expanded with extra levels like Psychologist, Interdyne and USSP for fork-specific factions and jobs.

- **Take** — Item-level ID restriction is the piece upstream genuinely lacks: it stops gear theft at the point of pickup instead of relying on players to respect job boundaries, and it gives security a real reason that a stolen ID is not a master key.
- **Skip** — The pieces are not self-contained: directional access has to be consulted from upstream's access reader, and the whitelist door check listens for a fork-only door event that upstream door code must be patched to raise, so grafting it means carrying permanent edits in upstream files that will conflict on every sync. The access-level prototypes are also tied to SS220's own factions (Interdyne, USSP) and are dead weight without them.
- **Touches** — security, command, medical, engineering, service, antagonist, all-players
- **Verified** — supported. I cloned the fork and grepped it directly. Content.Shared/Doors/Systems/SharedDoorSystem.cs (an upstream file, not under any SS220 namespace) is patched in place inside HasAccess(): it raises a fork-only DoorAccesAttemptEvent (consumed by Content.Shared/SS220/AccessWhitelist/SharedAccessWhitelistSystem.cs) and calls the fork's DirectionalAccessSystem.IsDirectionAllowed, both wrapped in '// SS220-directional-access' / '//SS220 ChameleonStructure' comment markers. That is exactly the 'listens for a fork-only door event that upstream door code must be patched to raise' claim in skip_because, and it is a real in-place edit to an upstream file, not just a hypothetical integration cost. The item-restriction (SharedRestrictedItemSystem.cs: cancels BeingEquippedAttemptEvent/BeingPulledAttemptEvent/GettingPickedUpAttemptEvent, popup + damage + sound on fail), the PDA/ID painter (PdaIdPainterComponent with IdCardSlot/PdaSlot and Chosen/Default EntProtoId fields, self-contained), and the extra access levels (Psychologist in medical.yml, Interdyne in interdyne.yml + access.ftl, USSP in ussp.yml) all read exactly as described.

**ephemeral-space**

*loop-change · needs upstream edits · medium confidence · 6 forks carry it*

The armory no longer opens with one ID: three separate hand-scanner switches ("Casper", "Melchior", "Yalthasar") are scattered around the control room and three different people must each flip one inside a short window, after which a station announcement counts down twenty seconds and the gates open. Get it wrong or leave one unpressed and everyone in the control room is shocked, an announcement calls out trespassers, and the switches lock out for a cooldown. Elsewhere, doors carry a printed emergency access code you can read by examining them, and an Emergency Access Terminal lets someone type that code in to look up a specific airlock and see whether it is bolted, powered and on emergency access, then toggle emergency access remotely. Lockers, doors and built objects can also be secured with a numeric keypad you punch a PIN into (and rewire with a tool to change the code), while a physical jammer item can be wedged into a door to keep it bolted shut until someone pulls it out.

- **Take** — The three-person armory switch turns "sec opens the gun room" into a public, announced, co-signed ritual that other players can hear, contest or sabotage, which is a real shift in how weapons enter a round rather than a new toy.
- **Skip** — The armory sequence assumes a map that actually has a control room with the switches placed in it, so it does nothing on your existing stations until you re-map them, and the keypad, emergency-access and emag pieces reach into upstream airlock, locker and construction prototypes rather than sitting neatly in fork files.
- **Touches** — security, command, engineering, antagonist, all-players
- **Needs** — [shared-utility-libraries](#shared-utility-libraries), [custom-station-maps](#custom-station-maps)
- **Verified** — partly supported. I cloned the repo and confirmed the core claims: the three named switches (Casper/Melchior/Yalthasar), the 20-second ArmoryOpenDelay, the 2.5s ButtonPressAllTimeframe window, the electrocution+announcement+2-minute-cooldown failure path, the emergency-access door examine text/terminal UI strings, the keypad PIN/rewire-with-tool mechanic, and the door jammer bolt-while-embedded behavior are all directly backed by the cited files. But the claimed 'needs-upstream-edits' downgrade from the seed's 'drop-in' guess is also independently confirmed: Resources/Prototypes/Entities/Structures/Doors/Airlocks/base_structureairlocks.yml (a vanilla-namespaced file, not under _ES/) is edited in place with an '# ES START'/'# ES END' block adding `ESEmergencyAccessDoor` directly onto the base airlock entity. That is a real in-place upstream edit shipped in the fork's own tree (fork-patches-upstream), and replicating the feature elsewhere would require the same edit to that codebase's own base airlock file (integration-would-require-upstream-edits) — both readings hold. Separately, I found the 'Lockers ... can be secured with a keypad' clause is not actually wired anywhere in the codebase (no Storage/Closets prototype has a DeviceLinkSink or keypad reference), so I flagged it as an overclaim.
  - unsupported: "Lockers, doors and built objects can also be secured with a numeric keypad you punch a PIN into" — the keypad only works by invoking a DeviceLink source port (ESKeypadLock/ESKeypadUnlock) against a target's DeviceLinkSinkComponent; only the base airlock prototype was patched with DeviceLinkSink-capable wiring for the fork's door work, and no locker/closet prototype in Resources/Prototypes/Entities/Structures/Storage/ has a DeviceLinkSinkComponent or any keypad-related addition. Storage lockers structurally cannot be wired to a keypad in this codebase as written.

**sunrise**

*loop-change · needs upstream edits · medium confidence · 6 forks carry it*

When the station changes alert level, an announcement warns that door permissions are being rewritten, and a short time later a second announcement confirms it: on red or gamma, security officers and the detective can suddenly open armory and security doors they could not before; on yellow, engineers get atmospherics. The same bundle adds walk-through scanner arches that ping and flash green or red as you pass and can be wired to doors or alarms so contraband trips a checkpoint, plus gear that simply refuses to work for the wrong hands — a nuke op rifle pops "refused" if a crewman picks it up, a hardsuit can be DNA-keyed to its owner, and some items check your tags before you can use them at all. There is also a powered "pacificator" machine that, while running, stops everyone within a wide radius from attacking anyone.

- **Take** — Alert levels stop being flavour text and start physically redistributing who can open which doors, which gives security escalation real mechanical teeth and gives scan-gate checkpoints something to enforce.
- **Skip** — It is not one feature but seven loosely related ones (alert access, scan gates, faction biocode, DNA-locked suits, tag restrictions, faction gear blockers, pacificator field) that happen to share a folder, so you inherit the whole maintenance surface even if you only wanted the alert-driven access.
- **Touches** — security, command, engineering, antagonist, all-players, cargo
- **Needs** — [abductors](#abductors), [modular-hardsuits](#modular-hardsuits)
- **Verified** — supported. I refetched all 13 cited files and they solidly back the gameplay description: ExtendedAccessSystem.cs (Content.Server/_Sunrise/ExtendedAccess) confirms the two-stage announcement-then-apply flow on AlertLevelChangedEvent; access_group.yml confirms Red/Gamma grant Security+Armory+Detective and Yellow grants ChiefEngineer+Atmospherics; ScanGateComponent.cs confirms scan-gate arches with success/fail states, sounds, and wireable SuccessSignal/FailSignal; BiocodeComponent/System confirm faction-gated item refusal with a popup; PersonalBiocodeComponent confirms a DNA field explicitly commented '// for now only for modsuits'; RestrictByUserTagComponent confirms tag-gated item use; PacificatorComponent/Systems confirm a powered, rangeable (32f) field that adds PacifiedComponent to nearby humanoids. Critically for graft_shape, I went beyond the cited paths and pulled Content.Shared/Access/Components/AccessReaderComponent.cs, Content.Shared/Access/Systems/AccessReaderSystem.cs, and Content.Server/AlertLevel/AlertLevelPrototype.cs — all outside any _Sunrise namespace directory — and each contains explicit '// Sunrise added' edits (the AlertAccesses dictionary field, the UpdateAccess method, and the ExtendedAccessOptions field respectively) that this feature's own _Sunrise code calls into. That is definitive proof the fork's own copy patches upstream files in place (fork-patches-upstream), and separately, grafting this into another codebase would require the same upstream edits (integration-would-require-upstream-edits) — so both readings hold. I also found RestrictByUserTagComponent.cs directly imports and is Access-restricted to Content.Shared._Sunrise.Antags.Abductor.SharedAbductorSystem, which independently confirms the claim's depends_on abductors is a real code coupling, not speculation.
  - unsupported: "a nuke op rifle pops \"refused\" if a crewman picks it up" — I confirmed the underlying mechanism (BiocodeComponent checks NpcFactionMemberComponent and pops a popup using AlertText, default "item-biocode-refused", cancelling the action) in Content.Shared/_Sunrise/Biocode/BiocodeComponent.cs and BiocodeSystem.cs, but could not locate the actual nuke-ops rifle prototype file to confirm this specific item uses the component; it's a plausible but unverified illustrative example.
  - unsupported: touches: "cargo" is not supported by any of the cited evidence files — none of them reference cargo, mining, or quartermaster mechanics; the only hit anywhere was an unrelated code comment ('// Sec owned by cargo.') in AccessReaderSystem.cs.

### Additional devices, gadgets and structures

<a id="device-and-machine-additions"></a>

Assorted new station hardware: handheld gadgets, device-linking hardware, holoprojectors, text screens, display cases, genetics consoles, sensor towers and soul-binding golems.

**rmc14**

*loop-change · entangled · high confidence · 15 forks carry it*

Instead of radio just working, players have to build and maintain the infrastructure that carries their voices. On the ground, comms towers and a sensor tower start broken: engineers weld the panels shut, cut and repair wiring, wrench the mast straight, restore power to the local APC, then tune the tower with an access tuner to add their side's radio channels — until that's done, nobody groundside can reach the ship, and the sensor tower feeds live enemy positions to the command map while it lasts (it randomly breaks again and needs re-repair). Where radio doesn't reach, players use a telephone network: rotary phones and wall phones are named after their location, you pick a destination off a tabbed list, the far phone audibly rings and emits a "starts ringing vigorously" emote, and whoever picks up hears you in a distinct purple anonymous whisper as long as you both keep the handset in hand and stay close. Command also gets an AI terminal you swipe your ID into to browse timestamped round logs by category, plus megaphones, a hand labeler, and squad-broadcast consoles that push announcements and map drawings to everyone.

- **Take** — The phone network and repairable comms tower turn communication itself into a contested objective — a genuinely fresh engineering job and a reason for command to leave the console — and the phone UX (named handsets, ringing emote, anonymous purple speech, hang-up on walking away) is a polished, self-contained interaction most forks have no equivalent of.
- **Skip** — RMC-14 is a total-conversion Aliens fork and this hardware is written against its own faction/IFF, access, squad and tactical-map stack; the ARES terminal in particular reads ID cards through RMC's faction system and pulls from an RMC-specific round-log pipeline, so porting it means either dragging those systems along or rewriting the plumbing, and the whole design assumes a two-site round (ship plus planet) where cutting radio is meaningful rather than just annoying.
- **Touches** — command, engineering, security, service, all-players
- **Needs** — [squads-ranks-and-skills](#squads-ranks-and-skills), [access-control-rework](#access-control-rework), [hud-and-status-readouts](#hud-and-status-readouts)
- **Verified** — partly supported. Fetched all three cited files directly. The two guidebook XMLs confirm nearly every specific gameplay beat: tower repair steps (weld panels, wire cutters, wrench, power, then Security Access Tuner to add faction frequencies), radio dead until repaired, sensor tower tracking unknown biosignatures on TACMAP and randomly breaking down needing re-repair, and the telephone system's named handsets, \"starts ringing vigorously\" emote, purple anonymous local-chat whisper while both hold the phone, and auto-hangup on walking away — all verbatim-matched. ARESExternalTerminalSystem.cs (plus a follow-up fetch of ARESCoreSystem.cs) confirms the ID-card login, category-filtered logs, and timestamped entries (\"dd - HH:mm\" format via CreateARESLog), and crucially confirms the entangled call: the terminal directly calls GunIFFSystem.HasFaction and reads Content.Shared._RMC14.Access's AccessComponent, i.e. it is wired into RMC14's own faction/IFF and access subsystems even though those live under the same _RMC14 top-level directory the path-scan treats as \"in namespace\" — exactly the kind of internal entanglement the claim used to downgrade the drop-in seed. That downgrade is correct and evidence-backed. Two flavor items (megaphones, hand labeler) in the gameplay prose have no support in the cited evidence or elsewhere I could check.
  - unsupported: "plus megaphones, a hand labeler, and squad-broadcast consoles that push announcements and map drawings to everyone" — the squad-broadcast/announcement/map-drawing part is backed by RMCGuideMarineCommunications.xml (Overwatch Console's Message Squad button, Groundside Operations Console announcements, Tactical Map Canvas-tab drawing broadcast to all marines), but megaphones and a hand labeler appear nowhere in the three cited evidence files and I could not locate them elsewhere (GitHub code search requires auth from this sandbox), so those two specific items are unverified.

**sunrise**

*activity · needs upstream edits · medium confidence · 15 forks carry it*

A grab-bag of new station hardware. The standout is the interrogator: security drags a cuffed or dead suspect into a powered upright machine, waits about thirty seconds of humming, and a ding announces that every removable implant has been pulled out of them, so a captured traitor loses their uplink and freedom implants without a surgeon. Alongside it are courtroom gavels that bang with a loud crack and shatter if you keep hammering, keypad doors and lockers that ask for a numeric code and beep angrily at a wrong one, cabinets that seal shut once you put something inside so only an emag reopens them, wall loudspeakers, disposal auto-loaders that batch items into one pipe cycle, admin-only hand teleporters that make cross-map or ghost-only portals, and a pile of new console circuit boards (cargo finance, station bank, salary, bounty sale, ERT call and approve, security fine records) so those consoles can be built and repaired rather than only mapped in.

- **Take** — Mostly additive hardware you can cherry-pick one item at a time, and the interrogator alone gives security a real, non-surgical answer to implanted antagonists that upstream lacks.
- **Skip** — It is a grab-bag rather than a feature, so half of it (finance, salary, bank, bounty-sale and ERT boards) is dead weight unless you also run Sunrise's economy and ERT systems, and several pieces sit in upstream namespaces (the disposal auto-loader and the sealing cabinet) so they need upstream call sites patched and will re-conflict on every sync.
- **Touches** — security, engineering, cargo, command, service, antagonist, admins
- **Needs** — [player-economy-and-banking](#player-economy-and-banking), [cargo-bounties-and-market](#cargo-bounties-and-market)
- **Verified** — partly supported. The claim's needs-upstream-edits classification is directly confirmed: Content.Server/Disposal/Unit/DisposableSystem.cs (a genuine upstream-path file, no _Sunrise markers) was edited in place to call the fork's AutoLoaderSystem.Cycle() at lines 90-127, a real in-place upstream patch, not a hypothetical wiring concern. Most individual devices (interrogator, gavel, keypad console, wall loudspeaker board, admin hand teleporters, and all the named console circuit boards) are confirmed present and self-contained additive prototypes/systems. But the flagship interrogator mechanic is mis-described: the code aborts extraction and immediately ejects the body the instant MobStateSystem.IsDead() is true (InterrogatorSystem.cs Update loop), so a suspect who is already dead, or who dies mid-extraction, never gets EjectImplants() called on them - the claim's premise of using it on a 'dead suspect' is contradicted by the code, and there is also no cuffed-status check anywhere (CanDropTargetEvent only checks HasComp&lt;BodyComponent&gt;).
  - unsupported: security drags a cuffed or dead suspect into a powered upright machine, waits about thirty seconds of humming, and a ding announces that every removable implant has been pulled out of them
  - unsupported: several pieces sit in upstream namespaces (the disposal auto-loader and the sealing cabinet) so they need upstream call sites patched
